records.text: 5 October 2026 Thematic Research Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG n In previous moments of contagion fears like this, it’s gone hand-in-hand with a sharp correction in risk assets. That happened in the European sovereign crisis in 2011-12. It happened again in the turbulence of the pandemic in March 2020. And it also happened in 2022, when rate hikes and a growth slowdown saw the STOXX 600 enter a bear market. n But this time around, despite the widest Franco-German 10yr spread since 2012, and the biggest weekly widening in decades, equities have barely budged. The STOXX 600 is within 4% of its highs, and the index “only” fell -1.1% last week. Those moves are not consistent with the scale of the spread widening. Elsewhere, Euro IG spreads have been remarkably calm, only rising to 101bps by Friday. That is far beneath their levels during the other periods of stress mentioned above, such as 2011-12, 2020, and 2022. n This simultaneous situation of sharply widening sovereign spreads, but limited equity declines and limited widening for corporate credit is highly unusual. In essence, we have rates markets pricing contagion and a significant hit to growth, which isn’t being reflected in other asset classes. That said, we think there is a high bar to activate the TPI and there may be other options for the ECB before that point, including verbal intervention, delivering or signalling fewer rate hikes are required, and/or pausing QT. Monetary policy tool not a fiscal one: The TPI remains untested but its mere existence has weakened the relationship between policy rate expectations and country spreads (Figure #). However, the the TPI cannot solve a fundamental problem. Moreover, there are a number of political-economy considerations that mean that its deployment is not straightforward. The TPI, first and foremost, is a monetary policy tool. Its purpose is to ensure that the ECB’s policy is transmitted evenly across the euro area. It is not intended to underwrite a member state’s fiscal policy choices or ease the burden on governments. This is why its activation requires “unwarranted” and “disorderly” market dynamics that present a “serious” risk to the transmission of monetary policy – a deliberately high bar. records.text: Operating profit As discussed above, we are expecting the group to continue to invest heavily in stores and marketing/events and as such expect less operating leverage than the sales growth would imply. The group’s reported operating margin came down 520bps in the three years from FY March 2023 to FY March 2026 (from 25.2% to 20.0%), and we see it going back to the c.25% level by FY March 2030 with gross margin accounting for two-thirds of the gains (or 190bps out of 310bps). Ten years out, we have gross margin converging towards a high 60s level and EBIT margin reaching the high 20s. Given EBIT margin hit a high of 25.2% in FY March 2023 with sales sharply rebounding post-lockdown, we think this is a realistic assumption. By division, in ten years time, we see Jewellery Maisons reaching a 35% operating margin, specialist watchmakers 14% and “others” delivering a (small) profit with the EBIT margin at 6%. Our FY27-29 EBIT estimates are 3-9% ahead of consensus. Other model-related comments While Richemont’s net cash position is already greater than annual EBITDA, we expect this to increase significantly to reach 3x EBITDA in ten years in the absence of exceptional cash returns to shareholders (such as special dividends) or M&A. This would put Richemont firmly in the camp with Hermès of chronically under-leveraged companies in the sector. records.text: Earnings, valuation and key risks What H1 2026 earnings tell us Sales: slowly but surely: Fashion & Leather was the main disappointment at the H1 results with organic sales growth in Q2 barely turning positive (+1%): Visible Alpha Consensus Data was expecting a tad more (+1.7%) and the basis of comparison (Q2 in the prior year had seen -9%) was optically favourable. Dior’s turnaround is proving very gradual and the group maintains that the goal for the brand is to build ‘lasting momentum’. It could well be that short-term disappointment makes room for a sustained rebound in the medium term. Conversely, lackluster growth in beauty (organic sales growth in the Perfumes & Cosmetics division was -1% in Q2) is linked, in our view, to the unwillingness of the group to expose its brands to an ongoing promotional spiral in the beauty sector. This is a simple reminder that, as a family controlled company, LVMH is able to consistently favour long-term brand equity building over short-term growth. On the positive side, Watches and Jewellery beat, with both Tiffany and Bulgari experiencing organic sales growth in the teens year-on-year, Wines & Spirits also beat, on better global champagne growth, a buoyant rosé portfolio and some signs of life in China for cognac. Subtle approaches to loosen financial conditions: Beyond this, we see a few more obvious and arguably ‘low profile’ policy decisions that could ease financial conditions somewhat whilst limiting potential political ramifications. First would be simply verbal intervention. For example, in the current market context, the ECB could reiterate that it has the tools and will not hesitate to use them should it believe that monetary policy transmission is impaired. The risk however is that this is misconstrued as signal for imminent action, and the market ends up testing the ECB. Second would be to issue a temporary pause on quantitative tightening. This would allow the ECB to reinvest the proceeds of maturing bonds back into EGBs, including OATs. Admittedly, the sizes would not be large (reinvestments in 2027 on average would be around EUR18bn per month and would be less targeted at narrowing country spreads than the TPI. In addition, it may send an awkward signal on the policy stance and the ECB’s views on the optimal balance sheet size. Whereas continuing QT while activating TPI would send a clearer signal on the intentions. That said it may be an easier first step that would leave the powder dry on more powerful tools. While the PP has an edge in the polls, it is unlikely to hold the parliamentary majority (176 seats) needed to approve a candidate for prime minister, similar to what happened after the 2023 election. At the time, the election results left the door open for the current PSOE+Sumar government, with parliamentary support from smaller independentist parties such as JxCat. The split in the polls leaves two main options for government formation: on the left, the PSOE+Sumar bloc might adopt the same technique as in 2023 and obtain support from smaller regionalist parties, although their relation ships have cooled in recent months. On the right, PP might try to emulate regional government agreements with the nationalist right VOX. If these groupings fail to approve a government by an absolute majority, a second vote will be held, where a simple majority is enough. This (unlikely) scenario would allow for the cabinet to approve/form a government through the abstention of the largest opposition party – a move that is only likely to be considered if the biggest parties agree to sideline VOX’s influence in a future government. If a government cannot be formed up to two months after the election, a repeat ballot is held. The last time this happened was in 2019. This is because while the number of cases in which inheritance taxes are paid when a person dies (percentage taxed) is rising, it is still only around 10%. Thus the direct benefits would go to these people. Also, because of the relationship to tax brackets, the larger benefit would go to cases in which the amount of tax was large. Thus there would likely be some type of limitation imposed on the tax-free threshold. The framework for life insurance is a useful reference. Currently, the tax-free threshold is ¥5mn multiplied by the number of heirs, and it would simplest to treat JGBs for retail investors in the same way. Then it would be possible to consider a new type of bond specialized for this purpose, in particular a super-long bond. In the market 30y JGBs yield above 4%, and even applying 80% of this a yield of more than 3% would be higher than the scheduled yield on life insurance. According to Life Insurance Association data, 1.24mn death insurance policies were paid out in FY3/25 with payments totaling ¥4,252.9bn, so the average per policy was ¥3.42mn, which was within the tax-free threshold. In fact, some people may have insurance in excess of the tax-free threshold and there may be more than one policy for some policyholders so there would be an incentive to shift to new JGBs. Most of the hardware investment is concentrated in the US and Asia, that together account for over 80% of the global net data centre additions. While vertical integration is a key characteristic of companies in the sector, we believe few companies within the sector have the same degree of control across sourcing, manufacturing and final distribution, providing both quality advantages and greater flexibility over product development. Second, we believe Zegna operates one of the strongest clienteling programmes in the luxury sector. The brand has built a highly personalised approach centered on its most valuable customers, combining bespoke offerings such as Su Misura (made-to-measure) with exclusive events and initiatives, such as Villa Zegna. This high-touch model has helped strengthen customer loyalty and engagement, with over 50% recurring customers, and in our view it remains a meaningful differentiating factor versus peers. Third, Zegna is increasingly exposed to a more resilient, high-end luxury consumer. Management has previously highlighted that for the Zegna brand, approximately 5% of its top customers generate around 40% of sales, with this higher-end customer cohort also continuing to outperform other clusters. Factors that could support a turnaround include: Greater stability in management and creative direction with a clear focus on n rebuilding brand desirability - even if it remains unclear whether the new set-up will translate into a brand comeback. The re-sizing of the retail footprint with fewer, better stores and an eventual curb of n outlets in the mix. The group’s ambition is to refurbish or relocate 2/3 of the network, reduce space by 20% (1/3 for outlets) and the number of doors by 1/3 with the intention of doubling sales density by 2030. At the end of H1, the group had shut 84 stores so is actually likely to end up being ahead of plan (a minimum of 100 this year) on this part of the reset. As per the following exhibit, Gucci is not the only brand that is part of this footprint shrinking exercise. The focus is on simplifying the offer (20% fewer SKUs) and developing icons for the n leather goods division, while keeping a strong mid-price proposition (€2-3k), a level we believe is more consistent with Gucci’s DNA, history and scale than its previous push further upmarket. The recent news of price cuts at Gucci on select bags and ready-to-wear items is both surprising (as luxury brands seldom cut prices) and logical given the prior pricing architecture. Bear in mind though that this was on a very small selection, and only on items labeled “still valid”, meaning these are not new products nor carryovers, but products from previous designers’ collections that have been kept.

This implies that even if high-end consumers adopt a “wait and see” attitude towards spending, there remain many consumers for these brands to recruit. We do not think “quiet luxury” is the future of the sector, as we expect a significant portion of sales to come from first-time purchasers who are seeking recognition from peers, colleagues, family members etc. However, it is clear to us that high-end brands have been quite resilient recently (as illustrated via the hourglass discussion above) and given their still narrow consumer bases, the visibility on growth is higher than the average for the sector. records.text: Clout - why scale matters Investors have been debating brand scale for a long time, with some defending the idea that small brands can grow quickly and others arguing that big brands can leverage their scale to build a moat. We side with the latter and believe that, in luxury, “big is beautiful” for three basic reasons: First, in the context of the adage that retail is about “location, location, location”, we believe that bigger groups (e.g. LVMH) and bigger brands (Chanel, Hermès) not only tend to secure better locations, but also benefit from lower rent as a percentage of sales. In consumer discretionary, the most prominent example is Apple, often the anchor for traffic within a mall and at times securing rent-free deals or otherwise favorable conditions in many Asia-based locations. Also, small independent brands historically relied on a strong network of multi-brand stores, both offline (e.g. the multi-brand stores in Italy 20 years ago) and online, and these have been gradually disappearing with very few exceptions (e.g. MyTheresa). This is another reason bigger brands dominate. Second, as social media expanded significantly in terms of usage and took precedence over traditional media, with COVID offering another boost, this has been an incremental visibility enhancer for the bigger brands that tend to attract greater consumer attention. of consumer spending. Regarding the household survey, though the unemployment rate (4.175% vs. 4.141%) edged up slightly, the U -6 rate fell by a tenth to 7.6%. The 78k rise in household unemployment alongside a 406k increase in employment had the effect of lifting the labor force participation rate (LFPR) a couple of tenths to 61.8%, its highest level since last May. In short, though the September employment report slightly disappointed, the picture of a stable labor market remains very much intact, particularly when coupled with recent readings from other key indicators such as ADP and jobless claims. Indeed, there ar e even some tentative signs of tightening in certain sectors. In turn, Fed officials are likely to remain squarely focused on inflation. We continue to expect two more 25bp rate hikes over the next couple of quarters. Wednesday’s release of the minutes to the September FOMC meeting may provide more color on the near-term rate outlook. The repricing in real rates reflects expectations of both a higher neutral rate and more restrictive Fed policy. Higher neutral is consistent with signals from equity markets, as the S&P is only 1% off its all-time high. The key question at this point is, how much further could the moves go? In the front-end, things are cloudy but arguably well priced. The spread of 2y over 5y5y real SOFR – a measure of expected Fed policy restraint – has risen in line with the curve bear-flattening, but is not especially high, even after adjusting for term premia. On the other hand, 1y1y (nominal) SOFR, at ~4.95%, is at or above levels that policy rules would call for with r-star of 2-2.25% and DB’s (or the SEP) projections for inflation over that horizon (see “How high might they go?”). We think the recent Nikkei 225 rally started with the unwinding of hedges accumulated in preparation for the equity market’s seasonal weakness in September. The market ended September without a deep risk-off phase, so investors are buying back cyclicals and taking profits on defensives. Furthermore, they are concentrating this risk money in quality growth stocks, whose earnings and creditworthiness tend to hold up even when interest rates are high. Technical tailwinds are also significant. The historical volatility of the Nikkei 225 and AI-related stocks began to decline with the dropping out from the three-month calculation period of the time of high volatility of AI momentum stocks that was concentrated from June 22 to the first half of July (Figure 1). For systematic players (including CTAs) that determine risk budgets based on volatility, this factor likely created a situation in which their holdings of Nikkei 225 futures were relatively prone to falling short and probably prompted a mechanical restoration of long positions. Meanwhile, we see limited room for TOPIX, which was less affected by the AI correction, to become less volatile. This difference is likely to support short- term Nikkei 225 buying and TOPIX selling. Wider spreads alone do not constitute disorderly dynamics and to the extent that wider OAT-bund spreads in part reflect a deteriorating fiscal outlook, are not necessarily unwarranted (at least directionally) either. At the time of writing, we do not think that the likely threshold for intervention has been met. Such threshold is inherently impossible to quantitatively pin down, as it does not depend on a level of spreads but rather a wholistic judgement call. A political problem for an apolitical institution: TPI eligibility (for more on which, see Figure #), rests on compliance with the EU fiscal framework, the absence of severe macroeconomic imbalances, a sustainable debt trajectory and “sound and sustainable” macroeconomic policies. However, these are non- binding and ultimately the decision on TPI activation rests with the Governing Council. This buys the ECB significant discretion – for example to intervene if the perceived threat to its ability to achieve price stability (for which financial stability is a prerequisite) is in question, regardless of compliance with the eligibility criteria. records.text: ECB—Potential Implications of Rising Sovereign Stress Rising global yields, persistent government deficits and increasing political uncertainty have put European sovereign risk back in focus, led by France. The 10-year French spread over Germany rose to 158bp this week, up 72bp over the last month, to reach the highest level since 2012. While sovereign concern has mainly focused on France, signs of spillovers into other bond markets have emerged, with the 2-year Italian yield moving up rapidly over the last couple of days. We therefore discuss the potential implications of rising sovereign stress for ECB policy. #1 Rates First, tighter financial conditions could have implications for the ECB’s hiking cycle. Our Euro area financial conditions indices (FCIs)—which include rates, spreads, equity prices and the broad Euro—have tightened notably in recent weeks (Exhibit 2, left). Our French FCI is now 53bp tighter since early July, with smaller moves in Germany (25bp) and a 36bp tightening at the area-wide level. records.text: The AI investment cycle continues unabated, with global AI investment exceeding n $1tn this year. While most of this spending is concentrated in the US and Asia, the global investment boom is showing signs of positive growth spillovers into Europe, partly offsetting headwinds from energy prices. In this Analyst, we review the evidence and estimate the likely contribution of the global AI capex cycle to European GDP growth. To do so, we leverage three different approaches. First, we allocate global n AI-related spending across countries and sectors by mapping the geographical distribution of new data centre capacity additions, assuming a spending mix similar to that of the US. We feed the resulting country-sector spending changes into a global input-output model to compute the direct and indirect effects of global AI spending growth on European GDP growth. This approach suggests that global AI capex will add 0.10pp-0.15pp to European growth in 2026. Second, we adopt a bottom-up approach that computes the domestic value n added of the European data centre build-out and of AI-related exports, which also points to an estimated AI investment contribution to GDP growth of around 0.1pp in 2026. Third, we examine granular industrial production data in AI investment-exposed sectors and come up with a similarly sized impulse to growth. records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Slowing construction activity caps market tightness: Despite a positive narrative from AI data-centre construction, notably in the US, sluggish construction activity globally has dampened zinc demand this year. Globally, we expect zinc demand growth to slow to 1.1% this year from 1.5% in 2025. However, we do not see slower global demand preventing the zinc market from slipping into a modest deficit in 2026. Clearly, though, zinc supply constraint has been the source of zinc price support, rather than a strong, positive demand narrative. We see little growth in Chinese demand in 2026, slowing to about 0.4% from 1.0% last year, as housing and commercial building construction activity continues to contract. In addition, Chinese vehicle production has fallen, down 3.7% y/y over January–August, adding to Chinese zinc demand challenges this year. The only positive has been the ongoing build-outof energy and AIinfrastructure in China. The US story is similar to China, with construction activity also flatlining in 2026. In addition, we estimate US auto production has contracted by c.1% YTD, but August levels fell by 3.5%, suggesting the slowdown is accelerating. As with China, energy and AI infrastructure have been key to preventing a significant zinc demand contraction in the US. We expect US demand growth to slow to 2.8% this year from 3.2% in 2025. records.text: Life insurance policy has deductible allowance of JPY 5mm/heir, which has not been changed since 1988. Equities are basically assessed at the market value, although there is a modest room of allowance as heirs can choose the lowest price among three monthly averages preceding death. JSDA (Japan Securities Dealers Association) puts out a regular petition to allow some hair-cut for assessing the inheritance value for equity, but has never been adopted. Therefore, if all JGBs are made inheritance tax exempt, not only a sense of unfair treatment among asset will grow, but also there may be a risk of hurting property market as the marginal tax goes up as high as 50% (Figure 4). Therefore, the government would need to consider the relative advantage of JGBs should not exceed much more than other assets. Trade-off between tax revenue and lower yield: Assuming that the most people who would buy JGBs for inheritance tax face 30% or higher more marginal tax, if MoF sells additional JPY 20trn JGBs, say twice the current retail JGB sales/year or similar to assessed value for 2025 inheritance tax, MoF would lose JPY 6trn tax revenue, which is translated as about 50bp interest cost on JPY 1200bn JGB outstanding (see Figure 5 for JGB interest rate payment and average %). Therefore, unless MoF feels that inheritance tax exemption will lead to more than 50bp reduction in interest rate, it is better off not changing the rule from pure tax revenue perspective. records.text: MediaStats Swedish inflation is firmer than it looks. Swedish inflation looks soft on the surface, but much of that is down to the budget. Cuts to VAT on food and electricity have pulled underlying prices down. September's inflation print added to that mixed picture: headline CPIF rose to 1.5% y/y, helped by energy, while CPIF ex -energy remained at just 0.5%, below expectations of 0.7%. The Riksbank itself describes underlying inflation as fairly close to target and expects it to rise, as stronger activity, a weaker krona and higher energy prices feed through. Business surveys agree, with services price expectations moving higher. Our daily PriceStats index adds to that picture, with monthly price momentum rebounding sharply since early September despite the softness in the official inflation data (Figure 2). If the pickup we are seeing carries through, it would reinforce the case for a November hike and suggest that the current Riksbank Nov26 hike pricing has room to grow. Figure 2 Swedish price pressures may be turning Source: State Street Markets Norges Bank looks nearly done . The picture in Norway is quite different. September's hike was the second this year, reversing last year's two cuts. But the minutes show a split committee, with some members preferring to wait for more data, which raises the bar for another hike. records.text: Japan Multi-Asset 05 October 2026 Citi Research 12 Japan Equity Strategy Flattening in yield curve As discussed in the macro section, we think the yield curve is likely to flatten as the rise in Japanese long-term interest rates ends, given 1) the market already prices in the BoJ rate hike pathway to a considerable extent so change in monetary policy is unlikely to constitute an additional catalyst for the bond market, 2) concern about the risk of a big increase in JGB issuance in the draft budget for next fiscal year has declined, and 3) there is an increased likelihood that the GPIF will change its asset allocation. In addition, changes next fiscal year to taxation of JGBs for retail investors are under consideration. In the government’s Basic Policy on Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform 2026, one clearly stated aim is to broaden the investor base by making JGBs more attractive to retail investors, with the MoF and FSA having proposed making them eligible for NISA investments along with other favorable tax treatment (taxation of interest income and favorable treatment under inheritance tax rules) as they formulate tax system amendments for the coming fiscal year. If such changes occur, we would expect a big improvement in JGB supply/demand. records.text: Van Cleef & Arpels: mono-design reliance not an issue just yet A key investor question is the level of risk with Van Cleef & Arpels so reliant on a single franchise, the Alhambra range (signature clover motif). We estimate this line alone represents close to two-thirds of brand sales, c.€4bn out of more than €6bn total. This puts the Alhambra range at a higher base than the highly successful and long-established Love range at Cartier which we estimate sales to be close to €3bn. We do not believe this is an issue yet as the brand is still developing broader consumer awareness and expanding its retail footprint. Separately, high jewelry is not a frequent nor recurring purchase, so we believe it is natural that when new consumers buy at VC&A, they would tend to buy what the brand is known for. Over time, VC&A has attempted to dilute the Alhambra dependence with the Perlée (beads) as well as Frivole (heart-shaped petals) collections, and while these might move the needle one day, we do not view the dependence on Alhambra as problematic. Base effects suggest even lower year-on- year average hourly earnings over the next two months. On a monthly basis, average hourly earnings would need to rise 0.41% in each of October and November for the annual increase to not fall further. Data like the Atlanta Fed’s wage tracker remains more important for judging underlying wage pressures and has picked-up over the last few months. But leading indicators suggest this measure still moving sideways over the next few months. We ultimately do think many Fed officials will still see wage trends as a useful signal for underlying cost pressures in various services industries. One issue is that high benefits costs could be keeping employment costs high overall even as wages slow. This may be evident again in ECI data released on October 30. Inside the model Sales We continue to forecast Brunello Cucinelli delivering one of the strongest and most consistent growth profiles in luxury, underpinned by a unique positioning at the very top end of the market and a highly disciplined approach to distribution. We forecast organic revenue growth of 10.1% in FY27E, 9.8% in FY28E and 9.5% in FY29E, supported by a combination of low double-digit retail growth and a stable wholesale channel. While store openings remain selective, we expect continued contribution from recent expansion efforts, a growing customer base and increasing average spend. Geographically, we continue to see significant runway in the Americas and China, where management believes the brand remains underpenetrated and where demand for highly exclusive products remains robust. We also note that Brunello Cucinelli continues to grow through both value and volume, a dynamic that remains relatively rare in the luxury sector. Operating profit We expect Brunello Cucinelli to continue generating modest operating leverage, supported by strong top-line growth and the completion of its major industrial investment cycle. records.text: Recent ECB commentary has started to highlight the importance of long-term bond yields and financial conditions for the policy outlook. Finnish governor Olli Rehn, for example, noted this week that the rise in long-term interest rates will slow growth and reduce passthrough of energy shocks to wages and prices. We maintain our forecast that the Governing Council will hike for a third and last time in December given pipeline inflation pressures from the energy shock (Exhibit 4). But tighter financial conditions reduce the urgency to raise rates beyond this, strengthening our view that the Governing Council is unlikely to step up the pace of hikes or take rates significantly restrictive. We therefore raise the subjective odds we assign to our baseline forecast to 60% (from 50% before) and lower the probability that the ECB hikes notably above 3% (from 35% to 25%). As a result, our probability-weighted forecast remains below market pricing. French sovereign spreads have widened sharply in recent weeks, a function of a wide fiscal deficit, a large accumulated debt burden, and no signal or political will for fiscal consolidation. Our economists recently raised their forecast for public debt to reach 125% of GDP by the start of the next decade (vs. 123% before). They now estimate that France will eventually need to run a 1% primary surplus to stabilise its public debt-to-GDP ratio, a feat rarely achieved in recent history and certainly not one being espoused by the main candidates on the left or right for France’s 2027 presidential election. Sovereign spread widening matters both for European stocks more broadly (as a signal of sovereign risk and political and policy uncertainty) (Exhibit 16) — and for French equities specifically. Each 10bp widening in the average spread of OATs and BTPs to Bunds takes 0.9% from Europe’s PE. records.text: 5 October 2026 Thematic Research Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG Conclusion: Bonds and equities are pricing different regimes, but the ultimate resolution will be decided by whether this financial stress begins to slow the economy. The last week has seen clear signs of financial market stress: n Sovereign bond spreads have widened as investors become more worried about fiscal risks. n The prospect of faster rate hikes has pushed front-end yields higher around the world. n Longer-dated oil futures keep rising, as investors price a longer closure of the Strait of Hormuz and extended disruption to oil markets. Because of all this, bond markets are starting to recognise that the collection of shocks we’re seeing are unlikely to prove temporary. This pattern has echoes of what we saw in the European sovereign crisis of 2011, the initial pandemic turmoil of March 2020, and the rapid rate-hiking cycle of 2022. In each case, there were clear signs of financial stress. Moreover, growth also took a hit, either via an outright recession or a significant slowdown. That backdrop meant that equities and other risk assets came under pressure as well. But today, we haven’t seen the financial stress cause wider growth spillovers so far. After all, it’s only just begun, and until recently it was plausible to argue that higher yields were also driven by strong growth. BAC, Buy: We remain constructive on BAC’s NII trajectory through 2026E/27E, and 2. view the high end of the 2026 guidance as achievable with potential upside as well, especially driven by a better NIM outlook. Further, given BAC’s asset sensitivity, and less exposure to capital markets revenue risk, we see an increasingly attractive top-line growth story. We see BAC’s NII growing ~7.5% YoY in 2027E, ~0.5pp higher than the large bank average for 2027E1 (Exhibit 44). We are ~1% above consensus 2027E NII driven by a combination of: 1) BAC’s asset sensitivity; 2) better than expected deposit repricing in a competitive deposit gathering environment, given it is not as constrained by funding; and 3) accretive fixed rate asset repricing, especially after the long end of the curve rose further in 3Q26. We expect expense discipline going forward, resulting in multiyear operating leverage; and 2026E operating leverage to be within the guided 200-300bps range at ~250bps. records.text: Margins: Quality of growth more important than pace: Management reiterated its expectation for revenue growth and margin expansion in FY27, despite remaining cautious on the macroeconomic environment. While gross margin may be slightly softer year-on-year in H1, owing to the normalization of inventory-related benefits and provisioning phasing, Burberry stressed that underlying profitability trends continue to improve, supported by lower discounting, higher full-price sales and ongoing cost discipline. What to expect for H1 results and what the market should focus on Bear in mind that, given the seasonality of Burberry’s business, H1 results (to end-September) are a small fraction of the annual results. Of course, given the volatility of the business post COVID and its repositioning, this might not be obvious, but as an example, last year H1 (to end-September 2025) accounted for c.42% of annual sales but only 12% of annual adjusted EBIT. While the current year may not be as extreme, our estimates have H1 (to end-September 2026) accounting for only 18% of annual EBIT (at £42mn). In other words, we believe it is important to avoid putting too much emphasis on such a relatively small number. H1 FY27E gross margin will likely be in line or even a tad lower than that of H1 in the previous year, we believe, as the group has benefited from some product provision reversals. Global and regional recession concerns are limited, and offensive quality growth is likely to be positively preferred at this stage. However, if credit markets in Europe and the US deteriorate further, recession concerns mount, and debates over a hard landing vs. soft landing become rampant, regional rotation could transform into global de-risking, and selling pressure could extend to quality growth stocks. This week, we want to confirm the Nikkei 225’s consolidating at 70,000 without a major reversal, a peaking out of the MOVE index, and US and European credit market conditions. We also want to use as a litmus test the group of Japanese stocks heavily owned by continental European institutional investors. If selling does not spread to this group of stocks, which has a relatively high proportion of quality-related names, we would safely assume that the Nikkei 225 is likely to continue to rise. Should selling be concentrated all at once, we would need to see if the turmoil originating in Europe has gone beyond a simple regional rotation. It is one thing knowing the market topping and bottoming signals and quite another to try to apply them in a practical sense. Visually, these things are compelling with a clear signal flashing, but false positives abound. Our experience has been that for bottoming signals, it has been easier to pinpoint the timing, with regards to a moment of capitulation. Even so, this is a process. It may be the case we see capitulation and re- establish only to see another leg down. All of this is effort, and our experience is that it is well worth it, providing an entry point much closer to the true bottom. In the recent period, the overall indices, as a whole, have not had the sort of pullbacks that trigger the broad bottoming signals. Only the ‘Liberation Day’ sell-off triggered a few. So we hold on to the bottoming signals framework, as we await the market conditions where it will be necessary. For smaller equity sell-offs where the VIX only goes to 20-25, these can be viewed as opportunities to re-enter at a better level, and using less stringent criteria than the Bottoming framework. One example of a rule for minor sell-offs: have vols rolled off the highs (through the 5d MA VG) and is a short lookback window (20d for example) holding in the S&P500? records.text: M Update 2 September ISM Services: Resilient Activity, Rising Prices Headline PMI & Main Message The ISM Services index (PMI) fell to 54.9 in September, slightly below the consensus forecast of 55.0. Among the four equal-weighted subcomponents, business activity and new orders fell meaningfully, while employment and supplier delivery times rose. The PMI averaged 54.8, 54.0, and 54.6 in 3Q26, 2Q26, and 1Q26. In September, 13 of the 17 services industries reported growth, one more than in August. Prices and supplier delivery times, in our view, were the two most important signals in the report. Tariffs and fuel costs were the most cited issues affecting supply chains in the survey. Fuel costs, in particular, were mentioned twice as often as any other single issue, highlighting the second-round inflationary effects of elevated oil prices. Supply chain constraints were also a top concern, putting upward pressure on both lead times and costs. The services sector experienced a sharp rebound post-COVID, fueled by pent-up demand, fiscal stimulus, and higher consumer spending on experiences, such as travel, dining, and entertainment, as restrictions lifted. This surge drove substantial job creation and strong activity across various services industries. However, growth in services has since moderated as the "catch-up" effect in hiring faded and the period of "revenge spending" by consumers ran its course. In our view, the quarter showed once again that Moncler’s business model remains highly resilient. What to expect for the Q3 trading statement Consistent with a weak summer and a “buy now, wear now” attitude of consumers, we believe Q3 will have been softer than an already weak Q2, before Q4 will show a rebound on product and the help of more space (thanks notably to the new Fifth Avenue flagship opened since September 10). The BoK began hiking in July and reached 3.0% in August on materially stronger, semiconductor-led growth broadening into consumption; we see two more hikes to a 3.50% terminal rate. In India, firmer growth and inflation led us to bring forward the start of the RBI's hiking cycle to October, with 100bp of cumulative hikes to 6.25% by April 2027. Taiwan's CBC is normalizing against resilient tech-driven output, and we see two more hikes to 2.25% by mid-2027. In Malaysia, we still expect BNM to hike as the recovery broadens, normalizing from a 2.75% policy rate that no longer looks like an equilibrium. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals5 October 2026 ab 12 How far could inventories draw? While global oil inventories have provided a critical buffer against the unprecedented supply disruptions in the Gulf, the market's ability to continue absorbing the shortfall through inventory withdrawals is diminishing. According to the IEA, observed global inventories declined by 507Mb, or 2.8Mb/d, between March and August, including a 99Mb draw in August alone. However, under our base case, we estimate implied stock draws may have averaged closer to 650Mb, or 3.5Mb/d, over the same period, with total inventories falling from around 8.3bn bbl in February to around 7.6bn bbl by end- August (vs. 7.8bn bbls by the IEA). Part of this discrepancy likely reflects reporting lags and limited visibility into non-OECD inventories. The IEA estimates "unaccounted barrels" in their monthly balance averaged +1.2Mb/d during July-August, suggesting observed stock data may not fully capture the extent of tightening in physical markets. records.text: e proposition could still trigger decent growth in the industry. Bull arguments would point to more balanced growth and structurally higher margins While luxury was heavily driven by Japanese clientele in the late 90s / early 2000s and by Chinese consumers in the decade preceding COVID, it is now a much more balanced sector with US consumer participation increasing and broad, wealth creation-based growth extending beyond one or two regions. As such, some might consider the sector today as somewhat de-risked relative to the pre-COVID era. It has increasingly become a global play on wealth creation, rather than on any single end market. Separately, linked to scale — sales are roughly twice now vs what they were 10 years ago with retail space not having evolved much — and more recently better cost discipline, we would argue that the sector is structurally generating higher margins now. Of course, as most companies are family-driven and think long term, one could argue that margins could go even higher, but benefits tend to be re-invested to fuel future growth. All in, we believe valuation is neither very compelling nor too demanding as bull and bear arguments are somewhat balanced, in our view. 4 October 2026 46 Goldman Sachs Europe Branded Consumer Goods: Luxury Goods For the exclusive use of CAYLA.BUETTNER@BLUECRESTCAPITAL.COM 7595159db82544668b3260609400172c

records.text: Hermès: A slowing growth algorithm; initiate at Sell, €1,350 price target We initiate on Hermès with a Sell rating and a DCF-derived 12-month price target of €1,350. While the share price has retraced meaningfully (down 36% YTD), we have reasons to believe the stock might continue to underperform peers. While we believe its top-line growth is likely to remain slightly ahead of that of its peers, we expect it will prove more muted than investors have become accustomed to: its historical double-digit year-on-year growth, quarter after quarter, has clearly come to a halt, in our view. The law of big numbers is a valid, but also easy explanation, and we feel the slowdown has more to do with weakness in the more volume-driven ‘métiers’ of the brand (essentially most non-leather categories) - these tend to be more exposed to the aspirational customer, as they do not benefit from the appeal of supply-constrained products. records.text: Industry overview - why muted growth won’t last and what valuation to pay A trifecta of issues being addressed slowly but surely Luxury growth has been weighed down since 2023 by three main issues, two of which, we believe, were within the industry’s control: First, macro issues. Amid the property market deterioration and high levels of youth unemployment in Mainland China, the psychological impact of tariffs in the US following “Liberation Day” in early April 2025, jittery equity markets, upcoming midterm elections and higher rates, as well as the ongoing Middle East conflict and other geopolitical tensions, there have been many reasons for consumers to cancel or postpone purchases of discretionary products. This has been unhelpful for luxury, coming on the back of two post-COVID years of exuberant spending, leading to a period of normalisation. We believe, however, that macro considerations have not been the main reason for lacklustre growth, but rather aggressive pricing and a slower pace of innovation, both potentially linked to a degree of strategic inertia. records.text: 5 October 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 48 OATs vs Everything Ioannis Sokos | Strategist | +44-20-754-75680 Note: This note was originally published on 28 September 2026. Over the past few weeks, we’ve used many different charts & models to illustrate the degree of underperformance of OATs. We usually try to account for the beta of OATs vs other EGB spreads or vs other risky assets in order to isolate the pure idiosyncratic component of this widening move. This is especially relevant lately, given the big moves seen in markets and the various external drivers, whether it’s ECB monetary policy, energy prices, outright yields or equities. Moreover, in our piece OATs – Lessons from History , we did a historical comparison of the current episode of OATs widening vs the Italian episodes in 2018 & 2022 as well as the French episode in 2017. The short takeaway is that the current OATs widening is already at or above the 2017 & 2022 episodes in France & Italy respectively, and only below the moves seen during the 2018 political crisis in Italy. We also argue how France in 2026 differs from Italy in 2018. In today’s FICOTD we present a rather simple but illustrative way of exhibiting the magnitude of the recent moves in OATs. There are no regression or betas involved, simply the spread of 10yr OAT vs a combination of different comparators, i.e. Bund, OLO, c ore proxy of DSL/RAGB/RFGB or semi core proxy of RAGB/RFGB/SPGB and the average EGB spread excluding OATs

records.text: US Economics 05 October 2026 Citi Research 7 (↓) We noticed a remark in comments from Fed Vice Chair Jefferson last week that we think is worth clarifying, as Fed officials may be underappreciating the disinflation that is still present in housing services inflation. Housing services prices, the dashed-and-dotted orange line, have been a source of disinflation in recent years, though that trend has leveled off this year. At first glance, year-on-year housing services inflation has moved roughly sideways since late-2025. But this is ignoring the technical issue that housing services inflation in PCE (which will be based on OER and primary rents in CPI) was essentially zeroed-out in October 2025 during the government shutdown. Housing inflation was then essentially twice as strong in April to make up for this missing data (and likely with a bit more catchup in May also from some possible missing November data). Annual rates of housing inflation from October through April would have been artificially too low due to missing data. Extrapolating the annual trend of housing inflation from September through May to correct for this issue shows housing inflation is still very much on a consistent downward trend. We expect this trend to continue based on the usual lag between housing inflation, new rents, and home prices, which have remained soft for well over a year. But last week’s Labour party conference, and particularly the headline speech from PM Andy Burnham, looks pivotal in having reduced stress ahead of Chancellor Healey’s 28 October budget. All of Burnham’s most ambitious plans – be it a reform of the triple lock on state pensions, a new, on-demand social care service or the possibility of re-entry into the EU – comprise his potential platform for the next General Election. They are not going to see the light of day before. As such, we think the rest of the month will offer few of the fireworks that had us concerned previously, leaving GBP to trade on fundamentals and rate differentials. While we doubt the Bank of England will be able to deliver on considerable tightening still priced into the curve, we are increasingly of the belief that only few others actually will. October 2026 Last month, we wrote that rates markets didn’t reflect the inflationary pressures ahead, with only limited tightening cycles priced in. We argued that, absent a fall in inflation, the pressure on rates would continue (link here). Since then, we’ve had a major bond sell-off, alongside clear signs of broader stress: European sovereign bond spreads have widened significantly; investors are pricing in faster rate hikes from central banks; and the disruption in oil markets has kept Brent crude above $100/bbl. Yet, despite all this, global equities are still far from correction territory, and the VIX index remains subdued. Credit spreads are nowhere near the highs of recent years. Even commodity curves are pricing a normalisation in oil prices for next year and beyond. So we’ve ended up in a situation where markets are pricing clear signs of stress, but not the broader consequences of that stress. As a result, we’ve been left with this divide across asset classes, with bonds pricing a fundamentally different macro regime from equities. records.text: Moncler: Superior growth and a tangible US opportunity; initiate at Buy, €62 price target We initiate on Moncler with a Buy rating and 12m price target of €62. Our price target is based on a DCF-derived fundamental value of €58.5 and an M&A value of €82, respectively accounting for 85% and 15%. While doubts on the sustainability of growth at Moncler have persisted since the IPO in December 2013 (e.g. “down jackets are a fad”), we are constructive on the long-term prospects of the brand. Stone Island, after years of brand repositioning, including an important distribution shift from wholesale to retail, is now a clear positive, albeit too small to really move the needle on the investment case. As explained, this expectation is linked to non-LV brands growing at forecast high-single-digit rates, with Dior’s repositioning the main driver (Loro Piana and Rimowa should continue their double-digit compounding journey while Fendi and Celine should revert to growth). Outside the key Fashion & Leather division, we see the strongest growth coming from Watches & Jewellery (+7% organic), with both Tiffany and Bulgari delivering good growth and selective distribution (+5%), helped by the continued success of Sephora, still partly fueled by space expansion, notably in Europe. We forecast quite pedestrian growth for the Perfumes & Cosmetics division (+2%) as we see limited growth outside Dior and Guerlain, and see LVMH continuing to avoid discount-driven channels. Finally, we see decent growth at Wines & Spirits (+5%) after years of digestion and inventory corrections. Earnings, valuation and risks What H1 earnings tells us Sales: signs of life, but not yet a turnaround: Kering returned to growth in Q2 (+2% organic), putting an end to 12 quarters of decline and benefiting from a clear improvement at Gucci, whose sales trend improved to -2% in Q2 (from -8% in Q1). The group saw solid performances from Bottega Veneta and Saint Laurent while Jewelry remained the positive outlier (+20% organic in H1). As Gucci, which still represents 38% of group sales, remained negative in Q2, management indicated that the group could see a broadly flat trend in Q3 despite substantial work underway on product, distribution and brand desirability. This implies another negative quarter for Gucci before, potentially, a return to growth in Q4. The key lesson from the results in our view is that Kering remains a ‘show me’ story, as we wait for clearer evidence that Gucci can return to sustainable growth, particularly in China, where management has acknowledged that rebuilding the brand will take time. Margins: Operational discipline delivered: Group EBIT margin increased 40bps to 12.8% in 1H, well ahead of expectations, helped by a 5% reduction in operating expenses despite continued investments behind the brands. Inventory reduction is progressing ahead of plan, with management reiterating its €1bn inventory reduction target and highlighting significant cuts to production volumes across Fashion & Leather Goods. Just as importantly, net debt fell from €8.0bn to €3.

The USD view in general and short EURUSD in particular hinge on whether institutions see fit to take incremental position risk from here, which is certainly not a given. So sharp was the USD buying last week that it closed not only the long-standing underweight but collapsed all position risks back to benchmark. If we sum the absolute values of our FX Holdings across the 37 currencies we track daily, we see that aggregate off-benchmark risk was only lower during the Spring 2022, just before aggressive tightening from the Fed and most other G10 central banks began (Figure 3). At that stage, we had only a small inkling of the hawkishness to come – now it is reasonable to question whether renewed hawkishness is at a peak. Nevertheless, that episode was marked by an initial repricing in skew for USD calls, then broader volatility across USD -based pairs and concurrent strength in the greenback itself. This time around, we have had the repricing in skew (Figure 4); whether history repeats and higher volatility and a stronger dollar follow as they did then are of course not guaranteed. But with the US in perhaps a better position to deliver tightening than the Eurozone at this stage, it leaves a USD long worth a look on a tactical basis. GBP event risks pass before they start. records.text: 5 October 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 30 Figure 44: Episodes of political uncertainty & ECB monetary policy Source: Deutsche Bank Research, Bloomberg Finance LP Methodology We assess the historical precedents through two lenses. First, we estimate the idiosyncratic relative-value cheapening of the domestic 10-year spread against other EGB spreads. Second, we estimate contagion to other EGB spreads by measuring their underperformance relative to other risky assets. For the first lens, we estimate the pre -crisis beta of BTP/Bund or OAT/Bund against the average spread to Bund of all other countries, using a period of roughly six months before the widening begins. We then apply that beta out of sample during the crisis period to estimate the idiosyncratic cheapening of BTP/Bund or OAT/Bund relative to the average spread of the other EGB markets. This captures only the relative-value component. If widening in BTPs or OATs also pushes other EGB spreads wider, the resulting contagion must be estimated separately through the second lens. For the second lens, we follow the same estimation process but regress the average spread of all EGB markets other than the country in crisis against credit spreads, using iTraxx Main and Crossover. By excluding the country under stress, this stage is desi gned to capture the spillover from the domestic shock to other EGB spreads. This exercise is an approximation and has several limitations. records.text: Valuation neither stretched nor compelling Over the past 3-4 years, luxury share prices have come down significantly, but so have earnings estimates. So, while valuations don’t look particularly attractive, relative to history, they do not look very stretched either. In short, the sector’s valuation appears unremarkable, but we think valuation alone is rarely a catalyst for investors to buy or sell shares in the sector. Instead, it is more a function of sales momentum, which we see picking up soon. As it stands today, forward PE for the sector is about 3 turns lower than the 15-year average of 25x. Bear arguments would point to limited growth and a threat of substitutes Bearish investors may argue that the sector should not trade in line with history given the past three years have seen much more limited growth if any than the long-term algorithm they had been used to for 20 years (c6-7% top-line growth on average). There are, however, a number of observations that support the idea that some brands may be better than others at incentivizing consumers to push the door. Moncler stands out in our coverage for its systematic approach to brand collaborations that seems difficult to replicate: the so-called Genius Collections platform. From the original framework in 2018 to augmented launches and, more recently, “co-creation” initiatives, Moncler has collaborated frequently with artists to engage consumers and reinforce the brand’s visibility. What distinguishes this initiative and sets Moncler apart from others is the frequency and complexity of Genius, which we believe may be challenging for other brands to replicate. Separately, the brand has ventured into large-scale experiential and cultural events (e.g. “the art of Genius” in London in February 2023 and “City of Genius” in Shanghai in October 2024) that are giving it a differentiated voice. We believe the challenge today is to think about the next phase of Genius. We believe that a strong culture of creativity is a hallmark of Hermès with the launch of 45k SKUs every year and the absence of a formal marketing department being a recurring talking point for the company. Lower realized and expected inflation should help compress breakevens across the curve, allowing the Fed to downshift from restrictive policy to neutral. The inflation breakeven curve, which is currently inverted, should normalize, with higher inflation expectations at the long end than at the front end. All else equal, this argues for marginally lower nominal rates and a steeper curve. However, faster productivity growth also raises expected returns on capital, which sustains high investment demand and reduces saving. records.text: A weak US labour print provided a circuit breaker: Global duration rallied and 10y OAT-Bund spreads tightened from 156bp to 141bp intra-day. A temporarily resolution in the Middle-East alongside factors that send yields lower could act as tightening drivers for OATs. Recently, flows took over fundamentals, especially at the front-end. The moves last week are likely not a good template for OAT spreads going forward. The price action in the past week in particular has been flow driven, rather than a change in the fundamental picture for France. Ordinarily, spread widening driven by fiscal concerns has tended to be led by longer maturities such as the 10y point. Last week, 2y and 5y spreads out-widened the 10y point, resulting in a sharp collapse of the 2s10s and 5s10s boxes. A blowout in front-end spreads can sometimes be reminiscent of default risk historically, but this was not the case last week. We think speculative longs in the 1y-5y sector for carry were stopped out or unwound in France and Italy. To add to this, we also observe that for most of September, the sell-off was futures led, likely driven by speculators, hedging needs related to Repacks, and technical factors such as a CTD switch on the OATZ6 contract which amplified the sell-off on the 10y point. Figure 3 shows a significant cheapening of the OAT basis (the futures contract underperforming the cash) which suggests the move was futures led.

records.text: Codes & Icons - what brands are known for Codes and icons are not necessarily big loud logos. They can be very discreet symbols that can only be identified by people familiar with the brand. Whether it is the signature woven leather technique at Bottega Veneta, the so-called “intrecciato”, the signature trench coat at Burberry, the best-selling Love range from Cartier or the clover leaf typical of the Alhambra collection at Van Cleef & Arpels, these products draw consumers into the store and provide a degree of social recognition, or simply the impression that they are buying a piece of the brand’s story and heritage. These are often products at the base of the brands’ pricing pyramid, as they correspond to a recruitment product along the lines of a “first branded handbag” or a “first branded watch” for a birthday, graduation, wedding or other celebratory occasions. With time, these ranges have evolved, offering higher-end versions as well as applications to other product categories. For example, at Chanel, the No5 fragrance, which is one of the key icons, was launched in 1921. Since 2021, No5 has also been a jewelry range, initially launched to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the fragrance, but now a reference point in that category in its own right. records.text: 5 October 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 43 A case for paying the belly Shoki Omori | Strategist | +81-3-6730-0835 This note looks at the 1y1y x 2y3y x 5y5y forward fly in yen OIS on three points: how to read its level, the regimes in which paying the belly is rewarded, and the shape of the recommendation. On Tuesday, 29 September the fly stood at -37bp (2 x 2y3y at 2.73% minus 1y1y at 2.27% minus 5y5y at 3.56%), which at first glance says the belly is rich. Against the chord joining the midpoints of the wings (1.5 and 7.5 years), however, the belly sits 3bp higher (+6bp in fly terms), so curvature is fair; the -37bp is the slope (-43bp) that a 1:2:1 structure with asymmetric wings carries mechanically. The question is whether to pay the belly. In spot terms that is a levered trade paying 4.6 units of 5y against 2y and 10y; it lost only about 4bp in September's front -led bear flattening, is rewarded by convergence to the house path (the house curve gives -27bp at end -2026 and +3bp at end -2027), and carries +3bp per three months, losing only in a super-long-led term-premium shock or if terminal repricing concentrates in the belly. Paying the belly looks like a trade: we add it at -37bp with a target of 0bp and a stop of -55bp. No valley, only slope On Tuesday, 29 September the OIS forwards were 2.27% for 1y1y, 2.73% for 2y3y and 3.56% for 5y5y, so the 1:2:1 fly was -37bp. records.text: 15 years later. The listing price implied a 12m fwd P/E in the low 20s, while it is now in the low teens. The listing in Hong Kong was consistent with a trend at that time for global companies to list there, hoping for a better multiple and justifying this with reference to the predominance of Chinese consumers in their growth profiles. Luggage leader Samsonite had listed there in 2011, while French beauty company L ’Occitane had listed in Hong Kong a year earlier. While the HK listing initially worked well, coming at a time when China was seeing strong economic growth and investors were ready to pay a premium for access to international brands, it has since been more problematic, in our view. First, it has meant that Prada has been listed on a market that has underperformed wider Asian and international markets, linked to more recent doubts over the Chinese economy. Second, and likely more importantly, it has meant funds with European mandates have not been able to invest in Prada’s shares, which have been left trading in Hong Kong with no obvious peer set. Samsonite and L ’Occitane have experienced these same issues. records.text: Earnings growth, earnings volatility, and valuation - L ’Oréal as a benchmark On September 9, 2026, the market cap of L ’Oréal surpassed that of LVMH for the first time in close to ten years (we have a Buy on L ’Oreal; see here, covered by Oliver Nicolai). We see this as an interesting signal for LVMH. Looking at certain metrics on a ten-year view below, we would argue that, theoretically, LVMH should be valued more highly than L ’Oréal. However, while LVMH has enjoyed higher sales and EBIT CAGRs than L ’Oréal over the period, we believe the volatility of its growth over the recent period (versus the compounding nature of growth at L ’Oréal) has led to an exceptional situation, and to LVMH’s forward P/E being close to 10 turns lower than that of its beauty-driven compatriot. We believe, perhaps counter-intuitively, that if LVMH were to deliver lower, but more consistent growth in Fashion & Leather (e.g., a steady c.3%-4%, instead of 6%-7% but with greater variance), the stock could finally start to re-rate. Ready-to-wear is similarly not dominant in most of the companies we cover with the exception of Brunelo Cuccinelli and Zegna. Like footwear, the complexity of maintaining different sizes as well as the pressure to clear excess stock at the end of a season are high. Within ready-to-wear, we believe outerwear is a compounding growth category that has been supported for a while by an elevation process in the US market and outdoor growth in Mainland China. This is one of the reasons we believe Moncler is well-placed in terms of sales growth. Watches, which are often combined with jewelry as “hard luxury”, have very different dynamics, in our view. The market is more male-driven than jewelry, usually still has a component of wholesale, and is a fully branded segment with a plethora of brands, within which Rolex is the dominant player. In other words, we believe the fundamentals of the luxury watch market are less compelling than those of jewelry. Aside from Rolex, in terms of market share, there are very high-end private brands (e.g. Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet, Richard Mille) and two sizeable brands: Cartier, part of the Richemont group, and Omega, part of the Swatch group. Late in a bull market, leadership quietly rotates from offense to defense well before the index rolls over. We track this with the relative strength of Consumer Staples versus the S&P 500. When the Staples/SPX ratio climbs above its 200-day moving average, defensive names are outrunning the market. On its own, the rotation is early and can persist for months, which is exactly why we pair it with the momentum confirmation above. There is also the possibility that continued technological imp rovements require ever -increasing investment. On the fiscal side, job displacement in sectors disrupted by AI could require greater public support, adding to deficits. In the most optimistic scenario, AI’s capabilities keep expanding and companies sustain high levels of investment without binding constraints. The market makes repeated upward revisions to expected productivity and returns on capital, and the investment bo om becomes a rolling investment cycle, sustaining upward pressure on r* and long-end real yields. records.text: “Inside the model”: A. Sales We expect a continuation of strong momentum across the group’s watch brands, with 2H26 cFX sales growth of 7.5%, broadly consistent with H1 trends. We assume Swatch continues to gain share in Swiss watches through the strength of Omega, Longines, Tissot and Swatch, helped by recent product launches and collaborations, while growth in China stabilises from depressed levels. While we expect growth in China to remain subdued versus historical levels, we assume ongoing strength in the US and stabilisation in key Asian markets supports group sales growth of 8.0% cFX in FY26 and 6.5% in FY27, before moderating toward the mid-single digits thereafter as the watch category remains structurally mature. B. Operating margin Our margin forecasts reflect a gradual recovery in capacity utilisation as volumes improve, while also incorporating management’s long-standing commitment to preserving employment and production capacity through the cycle. records.text: The other very relevant C: Chanel; a case study De facto industry leader growing faster than most It might seem unusual to discuss a private company in an equity research report, but we believe that understanding the factors driving Chanel is paramount to a broader understanding of luxury sector dynamics for two reasons: - First, the brand is considered a de facto leader of the industry with Louis Vuitton. While reported sales are a tad below LV’s (2025: cEUR17bn vs LV’s EUR20bn), we note that a) Chanel sells its beauty products and some of its watches and jewelry products at wholesale, meaning these sales would need to be grossed up at a retail level to make them comparable with those of LV; and b) Chanel’s reported sales do not include the Luxottica licensed eyewear products, which likely generate more than EUR750m (based on GS analyst’s assumption for EssilorLuxottica) per annum. In other words, similar to LV or Hermès, Chanel is viewed as a megabrand and a reference point in the sector. - Second, and more importantly, Chanel has been taking market share of late, and we believe it is worth understanding what it is doing right. While Chanel only reports once a year, a recent Bloomberg article highlighted that the brand’s sales grew 16% in H1 2026 with similar growth in its fashion division (by far the highest across the sector), lower growth in beauty (+8%), albeit still well ahead of peers, and substantial growth in watches and jewelry (+35%). It is important to note that

ll tell whether this approach will help Kering and its brands to regain relevance after a tough few years, but the approach is certainly unconventional and differentiated within the luxury sector. Centralization - While LVMH is often viewed as a collection of quasi-independent start-ups, the degree of centralization at Kering might come as a surprise. The challenge, as always, lies in striking the right balance. Prior to the new management team, some may argue that Kering suffered from excessive brand autonomy and insufficient coordination at the Group level. The organisation now appears to be moving in the opposite direction, with the creation of several centres of excellence at the group level, influencing the destinies of the different brands. As with the recruitment of executives from outside the traditional luxury talent pool, this represents a notable departure from Kering’s historical operating model and a more differentiated approach relative to many peers. At this stage, we believe it is too early to form a strong view on the effectiveness of the new organisational structure. Key hires for the centres of excellence include Stephane Noël as Chief Industrial Officer, Carlo Mocci as Chief Client Officer and Pierre Houlès as Chief Digital, AI & IT Officer. 4 October 2026 84 Goldman Sachs Europe Branded Consumer Goods: Luxury Goods For the exclusive use of CAYLA.BUETTNER@BLUECRESTCAPITAL.COM 7595159db82544668b3260609400172c

records.text: 5 October 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 14 Fixed Income Blogs Boom, gloom, or breakthrough: Mapping AI's three paths for rates Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Matthew Raskin | Strategist | +1-212-250-1741 Andrew Fu | Strategist | +1-212-250-1743 Note: This note was originally published on 29 September 2026 The AI boom is having a profound impact on US rates. The infrastructure buildout is lifting investment and overall economic activity while adding price pressures across computer chips, energy, and raw materials like copper. In the last month, both Treasury Secretary Bessent and Fed Chair Warsh have cited heavy corporate borrowing to fund the AI buildout as a factor pushing long -term yields higher. At the same time, the AI outlook has recently turned somewhat more cautious, with concerns rising around opaque financing, uncertainty over expected payoffs, and AI safety regulations that could slow deployment. In this note , we trace the effects of AI on growth, inflation, Fed policy , and the components of Treasury yields. We see the AI boom as bearish for duration and a flattener for the yield curve. A retrenchment in spending we believe would reverse much of that impulse. Over a longer horizon, successful adoption of AI could lower inflation while keeping real rates structurally higher. Global factors matter for OATs. An improvement in tone in the Middle-East, and factors that send duration lower could be worth by 15-20bp alone on OATs. Since the start of July, the 10y OAT-Bund spread has widened a significant 61bp. The widening has appeared to have had two phases 1) A global spread widening, exacerbated by the risk-off from the middle-east and higher yields, where the 10y OAT- Bund widened around 31bp, but Belgium and Italian spreads to Germany were also wider by around 13bp, 2) French idiosyncratic risk triggering a contagion to other EMU spreads and a flight to quality on the Bund ASW (see Fig 2). Up until the first phase, 10y BTP-Bund and 10y OLO-Bunds were around 15bp wider. Up until the second phase, 10y SPGB- Bund was around 18bp wider. Given the global widening across the regimes, we think around 15-20bp appears to be due to global factors widening all spreads. The price action on Friday showed us that global developments do matter, even in a day at first marked by sharp OAT underperformance. records.text: 157 ◼ Oil prices have rebounded on volatility surrounding newsflow on U.S.– Iran ceasefire. However, any concrete deal or conclusion to the conflict would bring oil prices back toward pre-crisis levels or even lower. The key risk here is that Energy equities have re-priced almost entirely in lockstep with Brent, leaving virtually no valuation buffer to absorb a pullback in crude. ◼ The strait or Hormuz remains a vital chokepoint, with approximately 20% of the world's oil supply and a significant share of global LNG transiting through its waters. Crude flows through the strait have recovered to 17.5 mbd or 98% of pre-war levels, while product exports remain at just 3 mbd or 58%, implying that the crude market has largely normalized even as refined product supplies remain constrained. ◼ Commodity strategy research suggests that, draws of crude oil and refined products amounted to 555 million barrels, only about one-third of what the commodity team had expected. Of the 555 million barrels released, the US accounted for 219 mb (excluding natural gas liquids), followed by China at 147 mb, Europe at 77 mb, and Japan at 69 mb. Compared to April, our commodity strategists now see a much less severe outlook. For now, there is still ample inventory to cushion a prolonged disruption before operational stress levels are reached, which limits the need for crude prices to move materially higher. Taking into account the possibility of M&A Across our global coverage, we examine stocks using an M&A framework, considering both qualitative factors and quantitative factors (which may vary across sectors and regions) to incorporate the potential that certain companies could be acquired. We then assign an M&A rank as a means of scoring companies under our rated coverage from 1 to 3, with 1 representing high (30%-50%) probability of the company becoming an acquisition target, 2 representing medium (15%-30%) probability and 3 representing low (0%-15%) probability. For companies ranked 1 or 2, in line with our standard departmental guidelines we incorporate an M&A component into our target price. An M&A rank of 3 is considered immaterial and therefore does not factor into our price target, and may or may not be discussed in research. Within this context, we have assigned four stocks — Moncler, Prada, Burberry and Swatch — an M&A rank of “2”, as we consider the possibility of them being an M&A target and as such approach a valuation that is 85% based on DCF and 15% on a takeout multiple. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals5 October 2026 ab 18 ability to absorb further supply shortages becomes increasingly limited, amplifying upside risks to oil prices unless Hormuz continues to normalise. In case of further and/or extended disruptions as we lay out in the scenario 3 and 4, inventories would need to absorb an additional 80-130Mb/month of supply losses relative to our base case, all else equal. This could push global inventories below 7bn bbl, increasing the risk that the impact of inventory depletion persists long after physical flows through Hormuz recover. In such a scenario, cumulative withdrawals could rise up to 1.8bn bbl, vs. 1.5bn bbl in our base case. Rebuilding inventories would therefore become a multi-year process, requiring 2.5 years of replenishment at 2Mb/d, vs. around two years under our base case. The implication is that even if supply disruptions eventually ease, the resulting inventory deficit could continue to support oil prices for an extended period. What we expect from the Q3 2026 trading statement As with the rest of the sector, we suspect the summer will have proven difficult for the Prada Group brands, with tougher comps in the US and South Korea, European growth dragged back by an absence of strong tourism flows, and worsening conditions in China. While the Prada and Miu Miu brands seem to be performing well in terms of conversion and events, the traffic weakness is such that we feel both brands will have ended up with zero growth in Q3. For the core Prada brand, we see flat organic sales growth, a similar performance to Q1 but a 600bps deterioration from Q2. Conversely, for the Miu Miu brand, which is less exposed to the US (higher growth market) and more exposed to China and the Middle East (tougher markets), we see brand sales declining 2% organically. A decline in Miu Miu sales would be a first since the days of COVID and certainly not good news for investors, albeit we think this negativity could be short-lived. On Versace, which has a much greater wholesale component, we believe the brand might add close to 10% to group sales with c.€135mn in sales in the quarter, a third being wholesale. Source: J.P. Morgan, Bloomberg Finance L.P. Credit markets are often the first to flinch. High-yield spreads, the extra yield investors demand to hold risky corporate debt, are the clearest real-time gauge of risk appetite, and they have a long history of cracking before equities at cyclical turns, as lenders reprice default risk while stock investors are still chasing highs. We don't wait for spreads to reach an alarming level, though, what leads is the change. We flag the signal when the three-month change in the high-yield spread is more than two standard deviations above its own one-year norm. An unusually sharp, fast widening that marks a genuine shift in credit conditions rather than everyday noise. We again pair it with the momentum confirmation, the red zones below mark where credit was deteriorating quickly and the S&P 500's trend had already broken. When risk-free havens and credit both turn while price momentum rolls over, it is a strong, actionable cue that the late- cycle backdrop is giving way. Continued expansionary fiscal stance: The change in the Takaichi administration’s messaging suggests that FY2027 bond issuance for the general account will likely be capped near JPY40trn. The actual figure could be lower, depending on the scale of the tax windfalls and the “Japanese DOGE” fund depletion. However, the headline figure is somewhat deceptive, as we discuss above. Much will be decided in the next few months, but we do not expect the administration’s underlying fiscal stance to undergo a major correction. While bracket creep amid elevated inflation will continue to exert a modest contractionary drag, we expect a moderate expansion of government spending, coupled with a consumption tax cut, to outweigh this effect. We expect the administration to maintain an accommodative fiscal policy amidst Japan’s near-full employment and persistent inflation. Accordingly, our outlook on growth and inflation remains largely unchanged.

Even as regional flows continue to recover, lower inventory levels are likely to create additional demand for inventory rebuilding once conditions stabilise. We also note that current inventory levels remain broadly consistent with Brent prices around $100/bbl based on historical inventory-price relationships. As a result, we expect stronger price support through 2027 than in our previous outlook, underpinning our higher forecast for next year even as regional flows gradually normalise. Given the unusually high degree of uncertainty surrounding geopolitical developments and supply normalisation, we are updating our scenario analysis with this note. While our base case assumes a gradual recovery in flows and easing tensions, we see Brent trading in an $80-135/bbl range across our scenarios. The path is likely to be driven primarily by geopolitical developments and the pace of Hormuz normalisation.
