records.text: Categories - some consumer verticals have better growth prospects than others We believe that what a company sells likely determines the type of growth that can be expected. Jewelry growth prospects being strong on the back of the unbranded nature of the category is an oft-repeated argument. But it seems that it is finally starting to be increasingly visible, likely linked to LVMH’s acquisition of Tiffany being a wake-up call for the industry five years ago and also the compounding success of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels within Richemont as well as Bulgari within LVMH. Outside of these four pure jewelry players, four mega-brands (LV, Chanel, Hermès, Dior) have developed jewelry quite well, and smaller brands, whether specialists (e.g. Boucheron) or generalists (e.g. Prada, Gucci), are investing strongly behind the category. Some might argue that we are in the later innings of growth for this category. We disagree and believe it has legs and good visibility. Beyond the mostly unbranded nature of the category, we like the fact that branded luxury jewelry is quite fragmented with the four specialists and four generalists dominating and there still being considerable scope for growth. The category is also helped by the fact that it is mostly retail driven (so no impact from de-stocking or restocking) while its customer base remains primarily female. records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 2026 ex-China mine contraction key to tightening zinc market : Spot zinc treatment charges (TCs) have collapsed since the start of the year, from USD50/t to −USD115/t, as ex-China mine supply losses mounted. Chinese concentrate imports, having surged by 28% y/y to 1.55 Mt in Q1-26, contracted sharply in Q2, falling by 8% y/y, reflecting the above-mentioned trends in ex-China mine supply. Given our expectation of a sharper downturn in mine supply through H2-26, notably ex-China, we expect spot TCs to be depressed through the rest of 2026. We expect smelter utilisation rates to drop during the rest of 2026 as a tightening concentrate market weighs. Indeed, we see Chinese smelters cutting production rates further through Q4, in part to try and provide support to spot TCs in the run- up to annual concentrate supply contracts for 2027. However, we still project full- year Chinese refined output growth of c.3% this year, rising to 4.3% in 2027 Ex-China smelters facing significant challenges: Ex-China refined zinc production contracted by c.3.6% y/y in H1-26, with sizeable declines seen in Europe, North America and Japan/South Korea. We expect full-year declines to remain at this rate, rising to a c.4% decline in 2027. Tiffany sales have been held back by the decline of both silver and bridal sales as it began focusing more on its four key icons (T, Lock, Knot, HardWear, the last two experiencing very strong growth) after its acquisition by LVMH. However, we believe this drag should start to moderate as, taken together, we estimate that silver and bridal collections likely accounted for close to half of the brand’s sales six years ago, while probably accounting for only c.20% of sales now. The elevation of the brand, combined with a very consistent effort to upgrade the retail footprint - 40% of c.300 stores now in the new concept, but with only about 15% of the US footprint (95 stores in all) done so far - has helped position Tiffany as a top of mind alternative to Cartier in many markets. records.text: e bigger brands that tend to attract greater consumer attention. Lastly, as the world has moved away from globalisation and become more fragmented economically and, importantly, culturally, only the bigger brands seem to have the means of financing channel or country specific products, media campaigns, and activations at scale. Whether it is the Olympics, F1, football at a global level, the opening of the “Louis”, a flagship of Louis Vuitton in Shanghai, or Cartier’s La Residence concept, few brands can support such initiatives without having scale. As an example, the recent Gucci F1 contract with Alpine will cost EUR150m, according to media reports, which is meaningful even for a brand such as Gucci but would be difficult to envisage for smaller brands such as Ferragamo or Tod’s. We see very few synergies in luxury, leaving aside real estate issues (negotiating power with distributors) and media expenses. But we do believe scale is a key competitive advantage in a sector that remains strongly driven by customer recruitment, rather than just repeat purchases. The caveat on scale, of course, is the rhetorical question of some brands being “too big to grow”, which we address in the LVMH section with regard to Louis Vuitton. The theoretical cap to sales that we are frequently asked about on LV, Hermès, Cartier and others has been convincingly addressed, in our view, by the noteworthy success of Chanel recently, a private brand, which appears to be growing quickly at present. 4 O

records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals5 October 2026 ab 21 4, we believe global oil demand could ultimately fall below the levels reached during the initial phase of the disruption, particularly as declining strategic inventories reduce the market's capacity to absorb further supply shocks. We see China as the key moving part in the global demand outlook. China’s response to the Hormuz supply shock has been more consequential than initially expected. We estimate Chinese oil demand declined by 0.8Mb/d in 2Q26 (20% of global demand destruction), before falling by 1.1Mb/d in 3Q26 (35% of the global contraction). We model its full demand down 0.6Mb/d y/y. While refinery activity has recovered from its June low and crude imports have gradually rebounded to 7.5Mb/d in September from the June trough of 5.9Mb/d, they remain well below pre-conflict levels of 10-11Mb/d. Much of the improvement has instead been driven by the easing of fuel export restrictions and stronger refining margins. Nevertheless, Chinese refined product prices have remained relatively insulated from the sharp increases seen elsewhere, while industrial activity has begun to stabilise. More importantly, despite healthy sales growth, the group continues to struggle to convert revenue momentum into meaningful profitability, highlighting the operational challenges that remain within the business. Margins: Margin recovery yet to be seen: The main disappointment of the results was profitability. Operating margin reached only 1.7% in H1 2026 despite solid sales growth, while net income amounted to just CHF16m on CHF3.1bn of revenue. Management continued to emphasize its strategy of maintaining production capacity and employment despite underutilization, arguing that stronger volumes should eventually drive a sharp recovery in margins. While sales accelerated in May and June and operating margin improved during those months, the expected improvement in profitability has not yet been consistently reflected in reported results. In our view, the results are likely to keep investor focus on whether Swatch’s fully integrated industrial structure is a long-term competitive advantage or whether it is affecting returns more than anticipated. Three aspects stood out. First, the SNB noted that the medium-term inflationary pressure had "increased only slightly" - a moderate upgrade from the June meeting, when it noted that this pressure was "virtually unchanged". Second, this impression was reflected in the conditional inflation forecast which was revised upwards only moderately; in particular the end-point at 0.9% remained lower than we had expected, especially when considering the recent CHF weakness and widening rate differential. Third, the FX intervention language was toned down. The SNB no longer said it had an "increased willingness" to intervene against "a rapid and excessive appreciation" and now just states that it is "willing to be active in the foreign exchange market as necessary to ensure appropriate monetary conditions."Overall, our takeaway was that the SNB has only very gradually tightened its communication. Ultimately this pace will determine the speed with which the sovereign receives credit-rating upgrades. We believe the current finance ministry leadership is genuinely determined to regain South Africa’s investment-grade (IG) credit status from all major rating agencies. Robust fiscal performance over recent years has already started to turn the tide towards upgrades and positive outlook changes (Figure 5). We think that a sustainable path towards IG credit will require real growth comfortably in excess of 2.0% over the medium-term, which as a base case, we only assume from FY28/29 onwards. The NT is acutely aware of this, likely noting that larger primary surpluses over the medium term are probably not a sustainable political solution in a country with such large socio-economic problems. This is revealed through a perpetually weak labour market and high degree of dependence on the state via government grants. We think the finance ministry is likely to start weighing these trade-offs more seriously as we get closer to the sovereign regaining IG status. records.text: ‘Inside the model’: Gradual recovery at Gucci, with margin expansion in focus Sales We forecast a gradual return to growth at Gucci, with organic sales growth improving from -3.6% in FY26E to +8% in FY27E and +8.8% in FY28E. Our assumptions reflect a rebound in brand desirability following the appointment of a new management team and creative direction, the benefits from product simplification, improved pricing architecture and a reduction in distribution. However, while early signs are encouraging, we remain cautious on the pace at which Gucci can regain market share, particularly in China where management itself acknowledged that rebuilding the brand will take time. Beyond Gucci, we expect Saint Laurent and Bottega Veneta to continue delivering solid growth, while Jewelry and Eyewear remain the most attractive structural growth opportunities within the portfolio. Overall, we forecast Group sales growth (cFX) of 1.2% in 2026, 7.6% in FY27E and 7.5% in FY28E, implying a recovery trajectory that remains heavily dependent on successful execution at Gucci. Our sales estimate for FY28 is +4% ahead of Visible Alpha Consensus Data, mainly driven by our growth expectations for the Gucci brand and Jewellery divisions, where we are 8% and 5% ahead of consensus for FY28 respectively. records.text: under either the PSPP or PEPP to lean against sovereign risk would likely be controversial. PEPP was designed as a temporary emergency purchase programme to deal with the fallout of the pandemic, while PSPP was aimed at lifting inflation during times of persistently weak price pressures. Stopping the unwind of either programme would thus risk blurring the lines between the ECB’s instruments and thereby likely raise legal questions. An alternative option would be for the ECB to maintain PEPP and PSPP runoff, while introducing new purchases designed to build up its planned structural bond portfolio. This approach would likewise slow (or stop) the shrinkage of the balance sheet but might fit better with the ECB’s objective of transitioning to a structural bond portfolio. A decision to do so could be linked to the ECB’s operational framework review. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 05/10/2026 06:01:08 GMT Distributed on: 05/10/2026 06:01:08 GMT 5 October 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Global Japan Rates Fixed Income Blog Date This note sets out a swaption trade for the Bank of Japan's October meeting (29-30 October). It covers four points: which meetings the market has priced for hikes, how rich front-end implied volatility is against realized, the 3m2y structure we build from that, and the risks and exit. As a tactical trade into the meeting, we recommend a 3m2y receiver spread financed by selling a payer. The market prices only 15% for October but a cumulative 24bp, almost one full hike, by the December meeting. Our economists expect no change in October or December and the next hike in January, so none of their hikes falls inside the window of a 3m option, which expires in early January. The options market is paying for the same place: 3m2y implied vol stands at 55.4bp, up sharply from 42.6bp at the end of July and at the 98th percentile since 2024, and 1m2y implied vol translates into a daily move of about 2.5bp, 1.7 times an ordinary day and more than the average move on BoJ decision days (2.2bp). Meanwhile the 2y rate three months forward is 2.06%, about 15bp above spot. We therefore buy a 2.06% receiver and sell a 1.81% receiver and a 2.31% payer. The package costs about 5bp of rate; it keeps +9.3bp if the 2y rate simply stays at spot and makes up to +19.7bp if the market reprices the pace of hikes t

Yesterday, we made the case for steepeners. A part of the argument was that Treasury term premia still look subdued by long-run standards. One framing we’ve long used in articulating a bearish view on duration is that the market is normalizing from the low -interest rate environment of the 2010s, as factors that depressed rates over that period are no longer operative (e.g., post - GFC deleveraging and risk aversion, concerns of secular stagnation, and global NIRP and QE). This informs our thinking on both the neutral rate and term premia. One way to visualize this is to look at current levels of 10y TP vs. their distributions over the period 1990 -2010. As the chart below (taken from yesterday’s note) shows, measured by that standard TP today are indeed quite low. While not included in the chart for ease of digestion, our 5s10s TP and the DKW model give similar results. (One exception is the VAR-based 10y TP measure from Fed staff.) records.text: Third, the ECB could activate its anti-fragmentation tools in case of extreme n bond market pressures. The Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT) programme was designed to support countries in a macro adjustment programme with potentially unlimited size. The Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) was devised to “counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics” that threaten monetary policy transmission. The TPI does not require a macro adjustment programme but is subject to several criteria albeit with significant room for Governing Council discretion. TPI activation would likely require significantly more intense and broad-based n sovereign stress, especially with inflation well above target. That said, the bar for TPI purchases to protect “innocent bystanders” from contagion (such as Spain) seems much lower than intervention in markets where current fiscal policies are inconsistent with the stabilisation of public debt (such as France). The TPI could possibly be used temporarily under disorderly market conditions to buy time for a policy adjustment (in a parallel to the mini-budget episode in the UK). Following recent drawdowns, US SPR inventories have declined to around 285Mb, 40% of the capacity of 714Mb nameplate capacity and the lowest level since the early 1980s. The US government has said that the SPR could potentially come down to as low as 70Mb. Industry estimates place the SPR's operational minimum inventory requirement in a wide range of 150-300Mb, implying that available strategic buffers are becoming increasingly constrained. With a further release, we believe the capacity of emergency stocks to offset a further prolonged supply disruption is likely to be materially lower than in previous periods of market stress.

That said, OMTs would come with stigma and, combined with the effects of the required significant macroeconomic adjustment programme, would arguably be politically unfeasible. Subtle approaches to loosen financial conditions: We see a few more obvious and arguably ‘low profile’ policy decisions that could ease financial conditions somewhat whilst limiting potential political ramifications. First would be simply verbal intervention. For example, in the current market context, the ECB could reiterate that it has the tools and will not hesitate to use them should it believe that monetary policy transmission is impaired. The risk, however, is that this is misconstrued as a signal for imminent action, and the market ends up testing the ECB. Second would be temporarily pausing quantitative tightening. This would allow the ECB to reinvest the proceeds of maturing bonds back into EGBs, including OATs. Admittedly, the sizes would not be large: reinvestments in 2027 on average would be about EUR18bn per month and targeted less at narrowing country spreads than the TPI, we think. Further, it may send an awkward signal on the policy stance and the ECB’s views on the optimal balance sheet size. Whereas continuing QT while activating TPI would send a clearer signal of its intentions. That said, it may be an easier first step that would leave the powder dry for more powerful tools. As for market topping, one might think we are trying to suggest much more active trading. Actually, just the opposite: we are looking to be more selective about our exits. With a market topping framework sourced from broad signals, we are looking to find agreement from a variety of sources: macro, valuation, technical, sector-based, etc. And topping is more challenging, since unlike for bottoming where the signals converge on a capitulation moment, topping signals may fire two years in advance e.g. housing starts tanking, yield curve inverting, etc. So a different approach is necessary. To deal with the different lead times, our approach is to have a checklist where we see how many topping signals have fired, and then to allow a responsive momentum exit rule to keep us invested as a tired market rally rises on fumes, and get out as soon as the momentum exit rule says it is done. By having a stringent topping framework, we are exiting less often, for broadly-sourced good reasons. Looking at a long term chart of stocks, we can see that stocks want to go up so long as the business cycle is going, so the goal here is to stay invested, and buy dips so long as that is the case. records.text: Rates Vol Lab 05 October 2026 Citi Research 2 Intermediate expiry vols have continued to outperform, and we believe it is partly due to hedging demand for MBS floaters with fixed rate caps. Intermediate vol looks high relative to long-dated forward curves, so we recommend shorting 3y10y vol against 10y10y/15y15y rate curve flattener. The 3y10y-1y10y vol slope also looks too steep relative to the level of vol. Intermediate vega looks high vs long-dated forward curves While the increase in overall implied vol has been notable over the past month, the real standout has been the relative outperformance in the intermediate and longer expiries. In long-dated vol for example, the increase in 10y10y over the past 2 weeks has been one of the largest since the GFC, and 10y10y vol is currently trading near its highest level in the past 15 years (Figure 1). The strong performance in long- dated vol has been partly due to the return of its positive directionality with rates amid the recent sell-off. records.text: 5 October 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 57 While the regulatory changes for SSA were substantial, we understand that some banks were asked by their supervisory authority to switch from the IBR - to the IBR-Foundation (IBR-F) approach for SSA. This might have led to more substantial increases of the risk weight. The IRB -F approach sits between the standardized approach (where all risk weights are fixed by regulator) - and the IRB-A approach (where all risk parameters are set by internal models), i.e., under the IRB -F approach numerous risk parameters are set by the regulator (for example, loss given default (LGD), exposure at default (EAD) and effective maturity (M)). We are not aware of changes in the treatment of SSA under LCR. Accordingly, as in the case of risk weights, most SSA continue from privileges under LCR rules, supporting SSA demand by banks for their LCR portfolios relative to private sector assets. The impact of changes for some banks due to applying the IBR-F is likely priced in. Overall, the main risk seems that banks themselves become more cautious from a risk perspective regarding certain SSA exposures. records.text: Growth is good, but Rates bite The rise in bond yields is hitting European stocks: STOXX Europe is down around 4.5% since the peak in early August. We see the sell-off as a function of the continued energy shock combined with the sharp rates re-pricing, the German 10-year yield is up around 35bp since early August and France is up 100bp and at 4.9%. The equity market is not immune to higher rates, with correlation between rates moves and the STOXX Europe having turned sharply negative (Exhibit 1). Since the start of the latest Middle East conflict, a 10bp rise in US 10-year yields has corresponded to roughly a 1.0% fall in the STOXX 600, while a similar move in German Bund yields has been associated with around a 1.2% decline. That said, as a small counter earnings revisions continue to be positive (albeit the change is small in front of the start of the Q3 earnings season) (Exhibit 2), and the economic data has been resilient and strong in the case of Germany and the UK. The link between earnings and performance has rarely been stronger. Over the past year, rising interest rates, the energy shock and uncertainty around the impact of AI have weighed on valuations across sectors (with Banks and Utilities the notable exceptions). As a result, sector performance has been driven entirely by earnings growth rather than multiple expansion (Exhibit 3). DV01 supply to the market from MinFin and BGK is already close to all-time highs, at PLN155mn (3m moving average, annualised), resulting in record-wide 10y ASW spreads (Figure 1). Crucially, the marginal buyer is far more price-sensitive at the back end than at the front. Foreign investors hold around 30% of outstanding notional in the 10y area, and while local banks remain the dominant holders of POLGBs overall, their positioning is heavily concentrated below the 5y point. The duration of local bank holdings sits around two years, well below the ministry's 5y weighted average maturity target. That leaves the back end comparatively exposed, with less sticky, price- sensitive demand standing in the way of further cheapening. This fits our broader bearish duration bias (see US rates: The Debt Knight Rises, 22 September). If fiscal sustainability becomes more of a live market theme, the back end should remain under pressure. records.text: uld lead to accommodative monetary environment The flattening of the yield curve normally occurs when the economy is expected to deteriorate and inflation to decline. However, this time around, if the drivers of flattening are a turnaround in yen depreciation, a decline in excessive concern regarding fiscal deterioration, and improvement in supply/demand deriving from changes at the GPIF and in JGBs for retail investors, it may not necessarily be linked to the economic outlook. In fact, policy constraints on long-term interest rates could be targeted at an accommodative effect, in a situation close to flattening due to yield-curve control. If policy successfully limits the rise in long-term interest rates and thereby leads to an accommodative monetary environment, it will likely be a tailwind for the equity market (Figure 19). The Japanese equity market has been susceptible to a correction since mid-August due to the rise in long-term interest rates and the yen’s appreciation. If the bond and forex markets settle again now that the FOMC and BoJ meetings have passed without turmoil, we would expect a rebound in Japanese equities thanks to strong fundamentals (Figure 20). Bringing It All Together We bring our estimates together in Exhibit 11. Our estimates of the impulse from the global AI investment cycle to region-wide growth range from 0.05pp to 0.15pp, averaging around 0.10pp for this year. Our input-output table-based approach that models the entire supply chain yields larger estimates, while a narrow market-based estimate sits at the lower-end of the range. Averaging the country-level estimates from our three approaches suggests that two groups of countries are set to benefit most from the capex cycle. First, countries that attract meaningful physical investment in data centres, such as Scandinavian economies and Iberia, are benefitting from domestic construction and fitting activity. Second, manufacturing economies integrated in the global semiconductor and electrical equipment supply chain benefit from incremental demand globally, including Germany, Ireland and the Netherlands. The AI boom and bearish case for duration The economic impact of AI is generally understood as a demand shock and a supply shock that arrive at different speeds. The IMF described the buildout as “a positive demand shock today and a positive supply shock tomorrow, rolled into one”. Fed Vice Chair Jefferson made a similar point about the timing of these shocks and inflation, noting that if demand arrives first, inflation rises, while if supply-driven cost reductions arrive first, inflation falls. The current buildout phase is primarily a demand shock, lifting rates through both real yields and short -term inflation expectations while also increasing term premia. The most direct channel is aggregate demand. We wrote recently that the competition to win the AI race is pushing firms to invest aggressively and potentially overinvest. Chair Warsh noted at Jackson Hole that business capex is growing at its fastest pace since 2021, with more than half attributed to the AI buildout. Competition for electricity, construction labor, computer equipment and other finite inputs is creating price pressures in those sectors. Another key channel is the equity market. Earnings have grown significantly across many AI -related companies, while equities of others are discounting expected future payoffs in the form of higher valuations today. Rising stock prices generate a positive wealth effect, supporting consumption outside of AI -related sectors

records.text: In essence, we’re pricing the symptoms of a new regime (e.g. yields at multi-decade highs and wider sovereign bond spreads), without pricing the logical consequences (e.g. lower growth and higher default risk) which have previously manifested in weakness for risk assets. This dislocation is unlikely to persist. Unless the financial stress of the last week starts to ease rapidly (a bit like happened in the aftermath of SVB’s collapse in March 2023), then risk assets will come under mounting pressure. So what are some of the biggest market dislocations right now? 1. Last week brought clear signs of contagion in Europe, with French and Italian sovereign bond spreads widening significantly. Yet risk assets in aggregate saw little reaction, with the STOXX 600 still only 4% beneath its record high. This is completely different to what happened in other periods of sovereign stress. n The moves in sovereign bond spreads last week were reminiscent of crisis periods. Last week, the Franco-German 10yr spread widened 32bps, the most in available Bloomberg data back to German reunification in 1990. Similarly in Italy, the spread over 10yr bunds widened 23bps last week. Duration implication for asset managers Asset managers use futures as long duration overlays and may find themselves unintentionally overweight duration. As rates rises, asset managers' long futures position can acquire more duration as the CTDs extend to a longer-duration security. As a result, investors may need to reduce futures exposure or rebalance hedge ratios to bring portfolio duration back in line with their targets. If we assume the empirical DV01 increases halfway to the longest DV01 point in the deliverable basket, asset managers' gross long position increase by $25mm DV01 and may require rebalancing. As for WN, the empirical DV01 is already trading close to the longest-duration security so rebalancing needs are lower, in our view. We estimate asset managers' gross long positions to increase by $3mm DV01. Long-end basis trading Market participants trading the basis can express views on future CTD outcomes based on rates and curve shape. Treasury futures do not have a fixed duration profile as it depends on the likelihood of bonds being delivered and probabilities assigned to those outcomes. In other words, futures pricing reflects some weighted probability of CTD outcomes and the duration profile is continuous over time and evolves as these probabilities change. records.text: Five reasons we believe the shares are undervalued We believe Prada is one of the most compelling growth stories in our luxury coverage. Unfortunately, we can identify many reasons that we believe can explain why investors have not taken as much interest as the fundamentals should warrant. We detail five of these here, and believe that if one or several of these can be addressed, this would likely unlock some value in the shares. Miu Miu landing The second derivative of top line growth has proven a strong support for shares in the luxury space. As we explained at the front of this report, we believe that sales momentum is more important than valuation, per se, when investing in the sector. The reverse is also true: while sales growth has remained decent at Miu Miu, and above that of industry peers, the deceleration of its growth has unsettled the market, leaving potential investors wary. As the deceleration has been visually very steep in H1 2026, and we believe will have continued in Q3, we think it is now paramount that growth stabilizes (or ideally picks up) from here, in order to reignite some investor interest. Holdings aren’t the only thing Industrials dominate in the world of BDCs. Industrials represent a large portion of future BDC maturities. These maturities are heavily concentrated between 2028 and 203 3, with Industrials accounting for 24.36% of all maturities during that period , equating to roughly $81 billion (Figure 11). The maturity wall for BDCs overall is very concentrated, so as we approach this period the current conditions for refinancing will become increasingly important. Fitch found that maturity extensions under stress accounted for 41% of all private credit default events, highlighting the importance of refinancing access for weaker borrowers. While many individual borrowers may be successful in refinancing their debt obligations, the sector’s large maturity wall comes at a time when signs of credit stress are already emerging across the market. Given the sectors growing share of PIK exposure, elevated non -accrual activity, and rising default rates, it’s large maturity concentration over the next several years requires monitoring. records.text: “Inside the model”: almost formulaic sales growth; sustained, high margins A. Sales Following a strong H1 (+9%), we expect Moncler brand growth to moderate in Q3 on softer trading trends before re-accelerating in Q4, supported by seasonality and store openings (notably the Fifth Avenue flagship). In the medium term, we forecast Moncler brand growth of 7.8% in 2026E, 8.1% in FY27E and 7.6% in FY28E, with growth supported by both like-for-like progression and selective space expansion. For Stone Island, we expect DTC to grow double digits for the remainder of the year and in FY27E before moderating to high single digits, and expect space growth to accelerate in the medium term. Our sales estimates are 5% ahead of consensus for 2028. B. Operating profit We expect Moncler’s strong top-line growth profile to continue driving operating leverage, although we see limited scope for meaningful margin expansion from current levels. Management remains committed to investing behind marketing, retail and infrastructure, while Stone Island’s development and the ongoing push to build a more ‘year-round’ brand should also require continued investment. As a result, we forecast EBIT margin expanding only modestly from 29.6% in FY26E to 30.5% in FY28E. While these remain among the highest margins in the luxury sector, we believe future earnings growth will be driven predominantly by revenue growth rather than further margin expansion. The idea was to assess the strength and duration of the FX and rates reaction after the event. In all cases, we found it was worth chasing the positive outcome after the event, particularly in FX (see Figure 3). Overall, the FX trade was profitable in the 1m–3m horizon (only the CLP posted a negative return one week after the first round). For rates, the result is less obvious. Only in Hungary was there a meaningful rally as there was a case for rate cuts (for the rest, rates were marginally lower, Figure 4). For Brazil, we decided to chase the move in rates as the BCB is going through an easing cycle and we see meaningful room for the market to lower its terminal rate expectation after yesterday’s election outcome. 205 October 2026 0.4% 3.6% 3.9% -4% -2% 0% 2% 4% 6% 8% 1w 1m 3m ccy move after elections after the election results avg max mi

In our view, the key question emerging from the results is whether Hermès can sustainably approach the double-digit growth profile that we believe investors have historically embedded in the multiple. Margins: exceptional, but not enough to offset growth concerns: EBIT margin remained very strong at 41% in H1, despite significant currency headwinds, while gross margin expanded by 40bps thanks to sell-through rates described by the company as exceptional, and disciplined inventory management. Free cash flow was particularly strong, increasing 18% as the group generated growth with favourable working capital trends. However, the resilience of profitability was largely expected by investors we believe, and was overshadowed by concerns around the top-line trajectory. Management continues to invest strongly in additional leather production capacity, planning to open roughly one workshop per year through 2030. However, the debate has shifted from margin resilience to the sustainability of growth. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 05 Oct 2026 11:12:40 ET │ 18 pages US Economics Inflation Weekly – What we learned from PCE revisions CITI'S TAKE Downward revisions to core PCE inflation were even larger than we were expecting, with year-on-year core PCE around 35-40bp lower as new methodologies for key components were incorporated. While not too far off from our ~ 30bp downward estimate, details were a bit different than we expected. Computer software and accessories prices are still heavily dependent on the same CPI component, while portfolio management services are now smoother month-to-month and more closely correlated with fixed income asset prices than equities. The recent move higher in yields could more directly help imply lower inflation in the next few months. We also think Fed officials are underappreciating that housing inflation is still on a downward trend and still a source of lower inflation. Many officials should also be encouraged by slowing wage growth that the labor market is not becoming a source of inflationary pressure. records.text: to argue that higher yields were also driven by strong growth. However, last week’s market moves demonstrated that this is no longer simply a “strong growth” story. For now, equities have been remarkably unfazed. And we know from the previous episodes above that the equity reaction can be delayed. For instance, in late-2021, even as central banks began to turn more hawkish and inflation was far above target, the S&P 500 and the STOXX 600 kept rising, and only peaked in January 2022. So there has been a lag before. For now, there are still hopes that this disruption will prove temporary, whether that's from fiscal risks, tighter central bank policy, or the inflation risk from oil. Indeed, previous moments of stress in recent years, like March 2023 around SVB’s collapse, ultimately passed quickly and did not cause a broader correction for risk assets. Nevertheless, it’s getting harder to justify these two realities at once. If the financial stress above continues, all the recent precedents suggest that risk assets will eventually come under mounting pressure, even if it happens with a lag. records.text: Versace acquisition Simplistically, we believe that having Versace in the portfolio is very complementary to the Prada and Miu Miu brands, given the substantial stylistic differences. Additionally, we view positively the use of cash to finance the transaction: use of cash tends to be a recurring question in the luxury industry as most balance sheets are under-levered. Nevertheless, we understand market nervousness around the execution of the Versace integration, notably in the context of the company’s historical M&A (see the following exhibit). We would argue the following though: We believe that the structure of the group today leaves it far better equipped to 1. integrate a brand than was the case in the late-1990s when Prada took controlling stakes in Helmut Lang and Jil Sander; and, A little like the situation with Stone Island within the Moncler Group, we believe 2. investors are spending a disproportionate amount of time scrutinizing the Versace brand transaction: three years from now, even in a bullish scenario, we would expect the brand to account for no more than 3% of group EBIT. Succession planning Succession discussions at the Prada Group have been unusually candid for a listed luxury company, in our view. The current plan is as follows: Andrea Guerra, a seasoned luxury executive known for running Luxottica for a decade and managing major businesses at LVMH thereafter, was brought in as group CEO in January 2023, when Patrizio Bertelli moved to the Chairman role.

records.text: The Governing Council has signalled that the list of macro eligibility criteria serves as an input into the decision and would be “dynamically adjusted.” The room for discretion in assessing the TPI’s criteria allows the Governing Council to activate TPI very quickly and unilaterally in the event of unwarranted sovereign stress. The objective of the TPI—to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics— suggests that significantly more intense and broad-based sovereign stress would be required for the Governing Council to consider activation. This is especially true in the current high inflation environment. Bundesbank president Nagel, for example, emphasised this week that the ECB’s instruments are designed for price stability and “have nothing to do with any specific yield spread.” We see a lower hurdle for TPI purchases to counteract “non-fundamental” fragmentation risk (ie, to protect “innocent bystanders” from contagion, such as Spain) than bond purchases in markets where fiscal policies are inconsistent with the stabilisation of public debt. That is, the Governing Council could decide to arrest spillovers from France into Spanish, Portuguese or Italian bonds, in so far the respective fiscal policies remain set on debt reduction, and indicate in its communication that it stands ready to do so. records.text: Comparing Hermès’ valuation to peers A little like Moncler, Hermès’ management has noted that the brand’s margin is already quite lofty, and consequently it has little intention of pushing to increase it much over the long term. records.text: Europe has outperformed the median in either US or Asia this year. But, nonetheless, the rise in bond yields is becoming increasingly difficult to n digest. The 6-month correlation — based on weekly changes — between STOXX 600 and the Germany 10y bund yield is -0.7. Outside 2022 we haven’t been this negative since the late 1990s. We find each 10bp rise in yields corresponds to roughly a 1-1.2% fall in STOXX 600. It’s not just yields rising but spreads too, European equities’ valuation has n historically tracked sovereign spreads and these have widened dramatically. Each 10bp widening in the average spread of OATs and BTPs to Bunds takes 0.9% from Europe’s PE. The good news is that the near-term prospects for earnings remain strong, EPS n momentum is positive, and Industrials, Technology, Energy and Financials (all large sectors in Europe) have strong structural tailwinds. The consensus expects EPS growth of 22% yoy in 2H, 15% ex energy. Moreover, Europe has a FCF yield of 5.5% vs. 3.5% for the US. Companies n continue to buyback shares and equity supply remains net negative. Europe is increasingly ‘being bought’ with M&A deals at highs. Domestic flows into Europe remain weak, but foreign investors are allocating as they seek to diversify. We continue to expect earnings to be the key driver of returns, and given n earnings growth is likely to slow in 2027 we prefer sectors where we see continued robust earnings prospects, we remain overweight in Technology, Banks, Renewables

records.text: Note that we do not believe the luxury sector is currently in a phase of consolidation and apart from some investments in jewelry (e.g. LVMH buying Tiffany, Richemont purchasing Buccellatti and Vhernier, Kering buying Raselli Franco), we haven’t seen much M&A activity of late. Whether for reasons linked to high leverage (e.g. in the case of Kering until recently), a change of culture or a willingness to focus on the strongest assets (e.g. LVMH and Richemont), we have seen more pruning within portfolios rather than additions. As long as growth remains muted and investor interest in the sector remains limited, we would be surprised if acquisitions were to occur in the next few quarters. Leaving aside exceptional circumstances (e.g. a family-controlled company deciding to sell) or any jewelry assets, we see scope for portfolios to narrow rather than expand. Given its cash position and the healthy state of both its brands, Moncler could be an exception and put cash to work on another brand if it finds one that fits. While existing luxury groups may not be acquisitive in the short term, we would not rule out interest from private equity which might have different considerations. Longer term, of course, as luxury demand picks up and companies think about diversification, there might be scope for M&A to pick up again eventually. Riksbank: Gradual normalisation with first 25bp hike to 2.0% in November The Riksbank left the policy rate unchanged at 1.75% in September, but is now guiding for a rate hike this year. With stronger growth data and more policy tightening abroad, we brought the first 25bp rate hike in our forecast forward from December to November. We then see the Riksbank pausing in December but hiking a second time to (an unchanged) terminal rate of 2.25% in Q1 2027, bringing policy to a likely neutral stance. From there, the Riksbank can then wait and assess how global inflation and interest rates develop and the economic recovery in Sweden unfolds. At this stage, we do not see the need for tightening into restrictive territory, assuming that the growth recovery does not overshoot and global inflation pressures ease into 2027. In summer 2022, another political crisis took the 10y BTP–ESTR spread to a peak of 188bp – we see that period as more comparable to today’s rising interest rate environment. Even then, Italy’s debt-to-GDP ratio was much higher than France’s today – at more than 138% after a peak of 150% in 2020. Shifting asymmetry: Lastly, a probability-weighted average of election outcomes, using current odds, suggests the 10y OAT– Bund spread could be in a 100–150bp range as we head into the election (see next page). We would argue that the 10y OAT–Bund high of 147.5bp reached 2 October on the spline suggests the asymmetry of risks is quickly shifting more bullish. After all, the far right may not win the election, and with the credibility of its fiscal plan still untested, may fail to entirely deliver on its (bearish) promises if it does win. How much more cleaning of positions need to come through will nonetheless remain central, while the global macro backdrop will also matter for the spread. records.text: The scale of tightening is more modest compared to the start of the year and when considering bank lending quantities, which so far remain robust. But the tightening in Euro area financial conditions is larger when measured with the ECB’s Macro-Finance FCI, which placed less weight on equity prices and the Euro (Exhibit 2, right). Tighter financial conditions imply weaker growth and, all else equal, fewer ECB rate hikes to stabilise inflation. Our estimates suggest that a persistent 100bp tightening in the FCI slows growth by about 1pp over the subsequent year. Weaker growth, in turn, lowers the chance of second-round effects from higher energy prices via increased slack and thereby substitutes for policy rate hikes. A simple calculation would suggest that the 36bp area-wide FCI tightening seen since the start of July might slow growth by 0.36pp, weaken inflation by 0.04-0.07pp (using typical “Phillips curve” estimates) and lower the required policy rate by 26bp (using a typical Taylor rule). Using the observed FCI tightening since the start of the year would halve the implied effect on the policy rate. Consistent with this, our past work shows empirically that tighter financial conditions typically entail lower policy rates, with a 100bp tightening in the FCI on average associated with a 80bp decline in rates over the subsequent year (Exhibit 3, left). These estimates would again suggest that the FCI tightening observed so far might roughly substitute for one 25bp rate hike

As a result, we would likely need to see more sovereign stress before the Governing Council considers steps in this direction. #3 Fragmentation Tools Third, the Governing Council could decide to activate its anti-fragmentation tools in case of extreme bond market pressures. The Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT) programme—launched in 2012 and never activated—is designed to support countries in an ESM-led macro adjustment programme by purchasing short-dated bonds with potentially unlimited size. The OMT’s requirement for a policy programme, however, entails significant political stigma, especially for large countries like France. The Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI)—launched in July 2022—does not require such a programme and is designed to “counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy across the euro area.” The TPI is unlimited in nature but subject to a number of eligibility criteria (Exhibit 7). These criteria require countries to pursue “sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies,” including (1) compliance with the EU fiscal framework, (2) absence of severe macro imbalances, (3) fiscal sustainability and (4) meeting the required country specific recommendations set by the European Commission. CRR III came into force on Jan 2025, with a few changes regarding the risk weigh of SSA. In our view, the impact on SSA was limited. For example, in our understanding, under the CRR sta ndard approach, none of the large SSA issuers was negatively impacted due to the regulatory changes. Hence, SSA continue to benefit from preferential risk weights, supporting demand by banks for SSA and public sector bonds in general relative to private se ctor bonds. This is the reason why banks focused on public sector lending typically have extremely high BIS capital ratios but also a high leverage ratio. Under the internal rating based (IRB) approach, there were no changes for central governments and multilateral development banks (MDBs) listed in Article 117/118 CRR. However, loss given default (LGD) floor of 5% for RLG -PSE exposures not treated to exposu res to central governments under the advanced internal rating -based approach (IBR -A) led to slightly higher risk weights. Also, MDBs not listed in Art. 117/118 CRR faced a small increase in the probably of default (PD) floor to 0.03% to 0.05%. However, the impact on risk weights was likely limited. records.text: Brunello Cuccinelli: Steady comes at a price; initiate at Neutral, €93 price target We initiate coverage of Brunello Cucinelli with a Neutral rating and a DCF-derived 12-month price target of €93. We view Brunello Cucinelli as one of the highest-quality and most consistent growth stories in luxury, supported by its exclusive positioning, loyal and recurring customer base and strong brand desirability. However, we view these qualities as largely reflected in the valuation, and, while we expect the group to continue delivering best-in-class top-line growth, ongoing investment is likely to constrain operating leverage and earnings growth, leading us to see more attractive risk/reward elsewhere in the sector. records.text: public-float rules were changed, enabling a listed company in Hong Kong (such as Prada) to use an alternative threshold principle to limit its free float to 10%, instead of the previous 20%. This is applicable only if the public float has a market value in excess of HK$1bn, which today would not be an issue for Prada (10% of its current float has a value of about 10 times this figure). Of course, reducing the float would not help the previous point we made about the daily trading of shares. However, it would present a means for family members, were they to consider that shares are undervalued, to acquire some at the current level, therefore increasing their 80% ownership. Earnings, valuation and risks What H1 earnings tells us Sales: Prada brand a solid growth engine: Sales growth at Miu Miu has remained positive (+3% in H1 and Q2 2026), but with its pace of expansion visibly normalising after the exceptional +40% growth delivered in Q2 last year. By contrast, the Prada brand accelerated to +6% retail growth in Q2, from flat in Q1, supported by like-for-like full-price sales, market share gains in China, strong momentum in the Americas and continued traction across categories. In our view, the most reassuring aspect of the results is that the Prada brand continued to outperform the broader sector, with management highlighting further opportunities in key markets. records.text: context. EM is at the center of this debate because EMs face the greatest risks of transmission of non-core to core inflation and, importantly, some EMs face a considerably stricter headline mandate. Indeed, our strategists recently wrote about the challenges in EM FX and credit markets given recent market moves. For most EMs, the response is to delay cuts, extend holds or increase the sensitivity of the reaction function to FX and inflation expectations; but we are increasingly seeing pivots to outright tightening. For economies where oil, FX, and the Fed path are key considerations, the first effect is less room to ease. In our forecast for Chile, we removed our December cut and now expect the BCCh to hold at 4.50% through year-end. Elevated oil and further Fed hikes outweigh a softer domestic growth picture, but that softer growth likely precludes a new hiking cycle. Mexico is similar. We expect Banxico to stay on hold through our forecast horizon: domestic slack keeps the bar for hikes high, while Fed tightening, sticky services inflation, and above-target expectations limit room for cuts. In Hungary, we now see the NBH on hold until December, with the external backdrop and October's budget framework likely to set the timing of further easing. Indonesia sits at the more acute end. records.text: Consistency - assessing the clarity of brand positioning In a post-COVID era marked by unsustainably strong sales growth, there was a tendency for brands to adopt similar fashion and align logos (see articles about the “Sans Serif Epidemic”), arguably losing sight of what made them unique in the first place. Five years ago, a Burberry shirt could have been mixed up with a comparable Balenciaga design in what ended up being a less differentiated sector creatively. Separately, some brands pursued short-term trends, regardless of what their DNA was. The most notable example of this has been Gucci. The brand was commercially successful under the tenure of designer Alessandro Michele and CEO Marco Bizzarri, more than doubling sales between 2016 and 2022 while adopting an exuberant positioning stylistically. In the post-COVID era during which the sector slowed down, digesting the previous boom phase, Gucci had a transition CEO and a new designer (Sabato de Sarno) following which the brand was repositioned towards higher quality, more subtle designs and higher price points, a positioning which we believe was not entirely aligned with the brand’s origins and DNA. A less distinctive voice is not necessarily a big issue when the tide lifts all boats. However, when the sector slows, as has been the case over the past 2.5 years, differentiation can become increasingly important. Topping signals Market tops are notoriously hard to call in real time: the index is usually printing new highs right up until it isn't. Rather than trying to pinpoint the exact peak, we assemble a panel of topping signals, independent, economically motivated indicators that each tend to light up in the late stages of a bull market, when risk appetite is quietly fading beneath the surface. In this section, we walk through these signals one at a time and show, visually, when each has historically fired relative to the S&P 500. Crucially, we never act on a topping signal in isolation. Late-cycle indicators are early and noisy by nature, a signal can sit "on" for months while the market grinds higher, and it often flickers, tripping for a few days, switching off, then tripping again. To keep those brief warnings from being lost, once a signal fires we keep it "on" for the next two months. We raise our Brent price forecast to $100/bbl in 4Q26, giving a 2026 Brent average of $92/ bbl, up $8/bbl vs. our previous forecast, and raise our 2027 forecast by $5/bbl to $80/ bbl. Following the breakdown of the US-Iran MoU, there has been much greater disruption to Middle East flows than we expected. While Hormuz flows have materially recovered in recent weeks, this improvement has come at great expense and remains fragile given ongoing Iranian attacks. We assume a gradual normalisation of regional oil flows through 1H27 on the basis of a similar arrangement to the June MoU by the end of the year but factor in a higher near-term risk premium as the path to normalisation remains uncertain. The longer period of disruption means a greater inventory rebuild from 2027, which should provide greater price support. We leave our long-term forecast unchanged at $75/bbl from 2028 but note potentially greater supply growth. Flows closer to normal but likely to remain volatile We estimate that oil flows out of Hormuz combined with bypass routes averaged >14Mb/d in September and reached nearly 17Mb/d in the past week, close to the pre- conflict level of 20.5Mb/d. However, a rapid decline in ex-China mine production through Q2-26 has changed the picture significantly .We now a expect a full-year decline in global mine output of 2.3%. We cut our ex-China refined zinc production forecast to reflect this sharp tightening of the ex-China concentratemarket, as well as outages, including at the 350kt/year Torreon smelter in Mexico, the 370 kt/year Sukpo smelter in South Korea, and long maintenance at Trafigura’s 290 kt/year Budel smelter in the Netherlands. Following an H1-26 contraction of 3.6%, we project full-year production to fall by 4%. For 2027, we expect mine supply to pick up by 2.6 y/y, principally driven by strong Chinese growth (+4.9%). As a result, we see increased reliance on Chinese refined zinc exports ensuring a balanced global market next year. Indeed, we expect the export arbitrage window, which opened in July this year, to open further through 2027. One implication of this is that our economic data projections, which leverage the relationship between fluctuations in financial conditions and economic data, point to a more severe economic softening. The projection now is for a decline to 1.4 z-scores over the next eight weeks (Figure 2). This corresponds with US GDP growth slowing by around 1.8%. E or T, or even R for recession? Our Market Policy Regime framework, which we often refer to as BERT, maps regimes based on financial conditions and growth expectations. BERT- implied (BERTi) is our method for extracting which regimes markets view they are in based on price action. Figure 3 shows the extent to which assets appear to be pricing each regime. records.text: In 2025, outbound travel from Mainland China to the seven key Asian destinations was up across all markets except Thailand. This year too, outbound Mainland Chinese travel is progressing well with the outlier being Japan as a destination. Note that individual travel (more relevant for luxury demand) is down less than group travel to Japan, but still -57% YTD in August. What growth to expect Glass half full or half empty? For the past 25 years, our luxury goods coverage has experienced average top-line growth of 6%. While growth has been pedestrian of late, we are still at sales levels that are beyond what a 6% CAGR would have implied since 2019 just before COVID hit. In other words, the bear argument that the sector may have gone ex-growth for an extended period is not one we agree with. While negotiation channels remain open, we see little sign of near-term progress. The approaching US midterm elections also have the potential to alter policy dynamics in either direction, further complicating the outlook. Hence, we think that markets are likely to continue pricing a premium to a certain extent until a more durable shipping framework around Hormuz is established. Under our base case, we assume that negotiations ultimately move back towards a similar arrangement to the June MoU by the end of the year, allowing for a gradual normalisation of regional oil flows through 1H27. However, we also see the path toward this normalisation is likely to be uneven given the uncertainty surrounding both the timing and nature of any agreement. In particular, unresolved questions concerning Hormuz controls, sanctions, nuclear concessions and other issues leave considerable volatility in both physical markets and pricing. In addition to the geopolitical backdrop, we also see inventory levels becoming increasingly supportive for oil prices. We estimate global observed oil inventories have drawn down by almost 750Mb, or around 4Mb/d, between March and September, leaving stocks below the lower end of historical ranges. records.text: #2 QT The balance sheet is in full run-off since the Governing Council stopped reinvestments of maturing bonds under the PSPP and PEPP in July 2023 and December 2024, respectively. Since then, the ECB’s bond holdings have shrunk by EUR 1.3tr and the level of reserves is approaching a level that the Governing Council might regard appropriate, raising the question whether the pace of balance sheet run-off could be amended to support sovereign markets. The Fed and BoE have recently adapted their run-off policies, too (Exhibit 5, left). One potential option would be to slow QT via partial reinvestment. For example, the ECB could maintain PEPP runoff (as these reflect covid emergency purchases) while reinvesting maturing bonds under the PSPP . Doing so would slow the average balance sheet runoff from EUR 400bn to around EUR 150bn over the next year (Exhibit 5, right). Moreover, the ECB could indicate that it intends to reinvest proceeds flexibly across maturities and countries, potentially providing support to front-end yields and supporting transition to a structural bond portfolio with shorter maturities. While the magnitude of reinvestments would be modest (eg, about EUR 4bn per month for France), this could provide an important market signal. That said, reinvesting maturing bonds under either the PSPP or PEPP to lean against sovereign risk would likely be controversial. While uncertainty remains, the sustained strength of corporate earnings driven by the AI investment boom suggests that FY2026 tax revenue could approach JPY90trn. Therefore, despite the consumption tax cut in FY2027, we estimate the government may be able to project tax revenue of near JPY90trn in the initial FY2027 budget, assuming a nominal GDP growth rate of approximately 3%. Nevertheless, the government needs to increase non-tax revenue for FY2027 by several trillion yen above the JPY9trn estimated in the FY2026 initial budget. One factor that could bolster non-tax revenues is the use of surpluses from the FY2025 settlement. If the administration avoids a large- scale supplementary budget at the end of this year, it can carry those funds over to the FY2027 budget. Another option involves transferring surpluses from the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account (FEFSA) to the general account beyond standard rules. We saw a precedent set under the Kishida administration in FY2023, where the government exceeded basic rules to increase transfers to the general account to secure defense funding. Even with these measures, a shortfall likely remains though, in our view. Swap spreads have been resilient in the recent sell -off, with 5y through 30y spreads sitting near their recent highs. This stands in contrast to past sell -offs, when sharp increases in yields have typically pushed swap spreads lower, particularly at the long end. There are a few likely reasons for this. First, equity markets have also been resilient to the rise in yields, and as we’ve noted previously, long -dated swap spreads exhibit similar behaviors as a risk asset. Second, Treasury’s intervention last month, together with the prospect of further actions, has helped put a floor under spreads. The impact has been more notable at the long end, particularly in 20y , which has disproportionately benefited from larger buybacks. Finally, market technicals, including mortgage convexity flows and corporate rate locks, have also contributed to wider spreads. The front end has behaved somewhat differently. 2y spreads have underperformed since the September FOMC meeting. Front-end spreads are less sensitive to Treasury debt-management decisions and more closely influenced by funding conditions and T-bill valuations. While Swatch has gained share, we believe that the underlying market in which it operates (mostly watches excluding Harry Winston) is a structurally challenging one, dominated by Rolex, a few independent high-end players and Cartier. We view watches as a somewhat saturated market, where wholesale exposure implies some volatility, as partners go through cycles of re-stocking and de-stocking. Separately, while the Swatch Group has diversified away from China and has seen very strong success in recent years in the US, it is still more exposed to China and the Middle East (through ownership of local retail chain Rivoli since 2014) than peers. records.text: Examining the long-term growth algorithm Structurally outperforming the industry, but no longer by much Hermès is the only brand we can think of (with the exception of Rolex which is privately held) which benefits from a structural discrepancy between supply and demand. Of course, some brands can be out of stock for periods - for example, Cartier’s launch of Love Unlimited in 2025, which saw consumers waiting for months - but the Birkin, Kelly, and Bolide handbags at Hermès have been subject to wait lists for a number of years, and are still in high demand. However, offsetting this, we see two negatives that have recently emerged, and which may not disappear anytime soon: First, demand for Hermès’ products outside leather goods has not been as resilient: these products are generally more aspirational in nature, and as such are more readily substitutable / prone to greater competition. Second, the price of a second-hand Hermès handbag has fallen quite a bit lately (c.12%-15% since early 2025) which might signal slightly reduced tension between supply and demand. Separately, as access to new handbags has been greater for high-spenders within the brand (who presumably purchased many accessories prior to acquiring the bag of their dreams), there is a risk is that these customers can access a bag on the secondary market without the substantial prior spending. Visible Hormuz LNG crossings averaged 21% of pre-war levels in September (from 4% in August), in line with total observed LNG deliveries from the Persian Gulf last month (Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2). We assume this supply adaptation improves further into winter, as a delayed version of what we’ve observed in oil, and we maintain our year-end TTF price forecast of 70 EUR/MWh (and JKM at $24.85/mmBtu). Despite improving ME supply, NW European LNG imports missed our September n expectations by 8 mtpa (13%) driven by LNG supply misses ex-ME and demand beats in Asia (Exhibit 3). Specifically, US LNG deliveries disappointed by 13 mtpa, at 118 mtpa in September, although the exceptionally high US deliveries in August (141 mtpa) suggest this was likely driven by a temporary shift in delivery schedule. On the demand side, LNG import beats vs our expectations were mainly driven by China (+7 mtpa) and South Korea (+6 mtpa), with China imports in particular potentially driven by misses in domestic gas supply growth while building inventory ahead of the winter. On the positive side, we believe that Burberry, now repositioned with more palatable price points, stands out as a compelling value proposition, certainly with a more democratic offering than some of its premium European peers discussed in this report. To that extent, it could benefit from consumers’ flight to value (something that has been very helpful for the likes of Ralph Lauren or Coach in recent years) as it taps the lower part of the hourglass-shaped consumption profile described before. On the flip side, the brand is likely driven by a more aspirational cohort than peers, and one that could prove less resilient if macro factors revolving around inflationary risk materialize more meaningfully. For the time being, it appears that the benefits of a return to its roots, and product/pricing that resonates with consumers again, are winning the day. However, there is a case to be made that its recent sales rebound might fade. This recent comments from several MPC members reinforced this message, in our view. Following the September meeting, we changed our BoE call and now expect the Bank to deliver two 25bp hikes, in November 2026 and February 2027, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%, versus our previous expectation of a prolonged hold with the next policy move being a cut rather than a hike. We think the 5 November meeting, coming after the Autumn Budget on 28 October, will be a good opportunity for the Governor to explain the decision, as it will include updated macro projections and a press conference. While we continue to believe that a weaker starting point for the economy and labour market than in 2022, combined with a restrictive monetary policy stance, implies limited risks of second-round effects, we now think reputational and risk management considerations will tilt the Bank towards pre-emptive hikes. In other words, we think the BoE will conclude that higher inflation and the potential hit to its credibility, would be more costly than tightening now and finding inflation less persistent than expected. Factoring in decent 2027E sales growth Product: We expect a flurry of new collections coming in store very early in the year for Spring / Summer following the many creative director appointments and brand reboot efforts. After years of relatively few reasons to visit stores, luxury consumers will have an incentive to push the door again. Chanel has been quick at re-setting, and others we argue will now follow. US: With China seeing its footprint being right-sized and growth dull both here and in Europe, brands have planned significant store openings in the US, both in existing hubs (NYC, LA, Miami) but also in those emerging (Phoenix, Dallas, Austin, the Hamptons). While space expansion continues, we are also convinced that brand awareness, which was low pre-COVID (with only three brands — LV, Tiffany, Gucci — exceeding 90 stores in the US), is likely expanding for most brands in the market. All in, we expect the US to once again be the outperforming market in terms of growth in 2027. records.text: The not-so long road to sustainable top-line growth Leather & Fashion set to grow again after a long drought, we feel While recent portfolio pruning (the long-awaited disposals of DFS and Marc Jacobs for example) is helpful, and we welcome renewed cost discipline that led to an H1 2026 EBIT beat, we believe a potential re-rating of LVMH’s shares can only come from a rebound in top-line growth. We see this as in the works, driven by a combination of stabilization of Louis Vuitton trends, acceleration of growth at the Dior, Fendi and Celine brands, and continuous compounding growth from the likes of Loro Piana and Rimowa. While the all-important Fashion & Leather division (>70% of group EBIT in FY26E) had previously seen seven quarters of consecutive negative organic sales growth, Q2 2026 broke that unfortunate series (albeit with a meagre +1%) and even if H2 2026 growth proves evasive (we forecast -1%, with Q3 down 2.5% and Q4 up flat), we expect better growth (+4%) to be visible in FY27E. records.text: l budget suggested the NT had been conservative in its revenue assumptions – see South Africa: Flatter curve pursued, plenty of dry powder in the keg, 25 February. Data from the first five months of the fiscal year (through August) supports this view, with cumulative corporate income tax receipts up 22.8% y/y, led by healthy mining profits (Figure 1). Despite disappointing macro conditions implying poor revenue performance, tax buoyancy is comfortably outpacing nominal GDP (Figure 2). VAT receipts have risen 9.1% year-to-date, and personal income tax is up 8.4%, and there appears to be very little fiscal drag resulting from the impact of the Middle East war. While the expenditure growth run-rate is tracking above 4.5% y/y – 2pp higher than the February assumptions – this does not indicate significant spending slippage. We estimate half of this increase is attributable to a reduction of the fuel levy over April–July, which cost 0.5% of GDP and was not in the original budget plan. The NT remains primarily focused on consolidation objectives, with a medium-term priority of higher primary surpluses and sovereign credit ratings upgrades. A further commitment to fiscal rectitude is expected on 21 October through a formal plan to legislate a long- awaited fiscal anchor. This will likely stop short of a binding numerical rule, and instead follow a ‘parliamentary procedures model’ as laid out in the NT’s May 2025 discussion document. records.text: 79.54 76.79 74.66 78.56 71.22 Consensus 86.65 84.26 81.46 77.00 73.73 74.83 70.45 Source: Datastream, UBS estimates The breakdown of the US-Iran MoU delayed the recovery in Hormuz flows and led to larger Gulf supply losses. Heightened Houthi activity in the Red Sea disrupted Saudi exports along bypass routes, reducing overall regional flows from late August to mid- September. Meanwhile, the US naval blockade effectively halted Iranian crude loadings, with no cargoes reported in September. We estimate Gulf supply shut-in increased to around 9.2Mb/d in August from 7.2Mb/d in July, driven by lower Saudi and Iranian exports. Since then, flows through the Strait have continued to recover and we estimate current flows rising close to below pre-conflict levels. Overall, we expect total supply losses to narrow slightly to around 9.0Mb/d in September, supported by higher dark- fleet transits through Hormuz and the resumption of loadings at Yanbu later in the month and recovering further through year-end. Despite the recovery in physical flows, we believe a meaningful geopolitical risk premium should remain embedded in near-term oil prices. Higher volumes moving through Hormuz improve overall crude availability but also increase exposure to renewed disruption if tensions escalate again. While the current supply risks have eased from peak levels, the current situation remains fragile and politically uncertain. records.text: Japan Multi-Asset 05 October 2026 Citi Research 19 Japan Real Estate and J-REITs Who wins the tug-of-war between rising rents and rising interest rates? The real estate sector has been underperforming since March. We believe the sector is underperforming because there is a clash between the tailwind of rising rents and the headwind of rising interest rates, and concerns regarding the latter appear to be prevailing. In fact, the number of BoJ rate hikes that the market has priced in has increased over the past few months, and long-term interest rates are also on the rise. Uncertainty about how high interest rates will ultimately go is putting off investors, we believe. However, once the 10-year bond yield peaks (likely around the 3% level) and there is visibility on the end point of the rate hikes, the impact of rising interest costs will become a “known known” , and concerns about a rise in appraised cap rates should subside. Given the near-term supply constraints, the momentum of office rate increases will probably accelerate, and we believe the tug-of-war between rising rents and rising interest rates will shift in favor of rising rents, triggering a re-rating of the real estate sector. However, while the meeting was clearly dovish, this does not mean that the SNB does not eventually want to tighten policy (not least because the SNB again characterized its policy stance as expansionary). The key question is timing. The September meeting clearly signalled, in our view, that the SNB does not see an urgency to raise rates as inflationary pressures are only gradually rising (and September inflation, at 1%, was in line with the SNB projections). Yet the gradual increase in the conditional inflation forecast and its upward slope, the SNB’s repeated remarks about the policy stance being expansionary, and better growth momentum (output gap now assumed to be closed by the SNB) point to eventual hikes to normalize the policy stance once conditions, notably the CHF, allow for it. So far, we had expected the first and only rate hike to come in June 2027. In light of our revised ECB outlook (we expect another ECB rate hike in December) and the associated wider rate differential we now expect the first SNB hike to come in March 2027 (to 0.25%), and we add a second hike in June 2027 (to 0.5%). We see the risks around this call as balanced: while higher inflation, more CHF weakness and earlier or more ECB rate hikes could bring forward the first SNB hike, there is also a scenario where the opposite happens (less ECB hikes, CHF strength, weaker inflation) and SNB rate hikes are delayed. However, this would require a government with a parliamentary majority that could quickly enact policy changes and would likely be viewed as political. Not the only tool in the toolbox: The ECB has a number of tools it could utilise to respond to the current and future market turbulence, but their design and likely impact vary. Both the TPI and Outright Monetary Transactions (OMTs) exist to address fragmentation risk, but while the TPI has somewhat softer and non-binding eligibility criteria, OMTs (also untested) require an ESM programme or precautionary credit line with strict eligibility criteria. The advantage of the OMT for the ECB is that it would put the onus squarely on Paris – since a credit line needs to be requested – as opposed to the decision sitting in Frankfurt. We would not be surprised if President Christine Lagarde – if asked at the October press conference – emphasises that both tools are available, and suggests that the TPI could deal with spillovers while OMTs are more suited to countries with unsustainable fiscal policies. In the past, the NT has tapped the Corporation for Public Deposits’ (CPD) cash balance, both as bridging financing during the fiscal year but also as a source of short-term borrowing across fiscal years – akin to issuing a bill. The NT ceased this practice in 2021, as the CPD also had solvency issues during Covid. If the NT were to use around 25% of the CPD’s cash as a source of short-term financing, this would release around ZAR55bn, as most of the CPD’s balance is currently parked either at the SARB or in the domestic banking system (Figure 9). This would also not breach the 15% limit on bills as a proportion of domestic debt as it excludes borrowing from the CPD. Because the term-premium formula includes a 20% beta to the 2y yield, it neutralizes the 5s10s credit-curve flattening described above. To preserve the potential asymmetry, we therefore prefer a 5s10s box trade to a relative term-premium trade. When the trade should work – and when it may not Timing is crucial for this trade, which is why we are initiating it only after seeing signs of bear flattening in the OAT curve and the contagion indicators described above. An unwind of any remaining carry trades in shorter OAT tenors could lead to more flattening. Admittedly, OAT credit -curve flattening began at a much tighter outright 10y spread than BTP flattening did in 2018. However, the starting points for BTPs in 2018 and OATs today are also very different. For a fuller comparison, see our recent piece OATs – Lessons from History. The trade should perform in a reversal of the recent OAT cheapening, with the OAT 5s10s curve flattening more than the SPGB curve. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals5 October 2026 ab 19 Do we expect more demand destruction? Demand destruction has so far been most pronounced in Asia, where the impact of the Gulf supply disruption has been felt most acutely. We estimate global oil demand contracted by 4.1Mb/d in 2Q26 (OECD -1.5Mb/d, non-OECD -2.6Mb/d) and 3.1Mb/d in 3Q26 (OECD -0.6Mb/d, non-OECD -2.5Mb/d). While we expect some lost demand to return in 4Q as Hormuz flows gradually normalise, the recovery could remain constrained by continued tightness in refined product markets, particularly diesel. According to Kpler data, global offline refining capacity moderated marginally in August to around 11 Mb/d from 12Mb/d July peak, but remained at historically elevated levels (see more details in our refining note). Overall, we forecast global liquids demand declining by 1.8Mb/d in 2026, (excl. biofuels and NGL at -0.7Mb/d) before rebounding by 2.8Mb/d in 2027. Europe remains particularly exposed to the ongoing diesel squeeze, which we estimate accounts for a large share of the region’s 0.3Mb/d y/y demand decline in 2026. The pressure could intensify if the US bans diesel exports. Russia has already extended its diesel export ban through October (link), and China started to reduce fuel exports to preserve domestic stocks (link).
