records.text: Anthi Tsouvali, Macro Strategy Team 6 October 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Global Equity Strategy US Industrials are running out of steam In a sea of risks, equity markets remain resilient and cyclicals are outperforming defensives. US Industrials however have struggled over the last three months : now institutional investors have built very large underweight positions but continue to sell . That seems odd for a sector that has been benefitting from the AI buildout and increasing defence spending, but it has come more apparent recently that prices and expectations have go tten ahead of themselves, as most of the demand has been pushed further out into the future. As valuations remain extended, and earnings continue to drop, we see no reason to buy the sector. Equity risk appetite still intact. Bond yields around the world are trading at multi-decade highs as markets are once again focused on persistent inflation, heavy debt issuance and a resilient economy that has given the Fed the green light to further rate hikes. While US Treasury yields are moving higher and bond volatility has increased, equity markets remain almost unfazed, anticipating the start of the 3Q earnings reporting season. Our proprietary behavioural indicators show exactly that. While overall risk appetite has recently weakened , demand for risky equities remains intact. In fact, institutional investors continue to allocate more on equities versus bonds and cash (Figure 1). Industrials

More importantly, management highlighted continued double-digit DTC growth at the Zegna brand through July and August, alongside ongoing market share gains in China. records.text: ‘Inside the model’: solid Prada, Miu Miu pick-up, Versace integration and some margin expansion Sales We forecast limited growth excluding Versace in FY26E (+1% reported), reflecting the significant slowdown at Miu Miu and a more challenging industry backdrop. Beyond FY26E, we assume a relatively solid growth profile for both Prada and a moderation for Miu Miu retail sales. For the Prada brand, we forecast c.5% cFX retail growth annually, reflecting continued brand strength but a more measured growth algorithm than in recent years. For Miu Miu, we assume growth normalises towards a mid-single digit level following the exceptional expansion of the past four years, with retail sales growing 6% in FY27E and 5% thereafter. Finally, we assume a gradual recovery at Versace, with growth initially modest as distribution is reset, before accelerating as the product offering, distribution and brand positioning are refreshed under the new creative direction. Overall, we believe our forecasts imply a recovery that is realistic rather than aggressive, and therefore leaves room for upside should Miu Miu stabilise at a higher growth rate or Prada continue to outperform the broader luxury sector. Operating profit We expect Prada’s earnings growth to be driven primarily by operating leverage and a gradual reduction in the drag from Versace. Japanese equity market sentiment also remains in neutral territory, far from total optimism. In assessing regional sentiment as well, we think that rather than a simple risk-on environment, risk money is moving selectively in search of regions and stocks globally that can balance rising interest rates and stock prices. In terms of CTA regional equity futures positions as well, European equities were sold in the week through October 2, while funds returned to the NASDAQ, TAIEX, and Nikkei 225 (Figure 9). Furthermore, in light of bond futures positions also, bond shorts and equity longs have coexisted in the Japanese and the US markets since September 1. In contrast, the accumulation of bond shorts and equity selling are proceeding simultaneously in the French, German, and Australian markets (Figure 10). Funds may be moving from regions where the coexistence of rising interest rates and stock prices has become difficult to the US and Japanese markets, where they are still seen as compatible. The top 7 banks have an estimated ~$78bn of excess capital based on target requirements as of now, but if we factor in the higher G-SIB buffers as of 2Q26, and assuming no mitigation, excess capital is significantly lower. There has been continued pressure on G-SIB scores, with G-SIB buffers on average expected to increase 120bps by 2029E, with none of the top 5 banks expected to be able to mitigate G-SIB scores sufficiently to come down a G-SIB bucket by year-end 2026 (based on historical mitigation trends). Furthermore, 7-year UST yields were up 89bps in 3Q26, which results in negative marks on AFS securities for banks. That being said, we believe banks will face only a modest 8bps TCE impact from AFS impact of higher rates. Notably, USB paused its buybacks in 3Q26, partially driven by higher rates. We now forecast 2026E/27E/28E buybacks up 5%/13%/17% YoY for the large banks. Valuation After a 5% decline in stock prices in 3Q26, driven by multiple derating, partially offset by estimate upgrades, we believe the group is fairly valued, with ~11.0x FY+2 P/Es, currently around historical levels (~50th %ile over the past decade), and the group trading at 60% of the S&P 500 multiple, 1pp below the historical relationship to the S&P 500’s multiple. Those with this view are often critical of the government outlook that fiscal policy can boost the potential growth rate. We have no answer to the difference in these theoretical standpoints, but the Takaichi government adopts the positive view. Growth rates cannot be confirmed until at least several years later, and growth in productivity needs to exceed the rate of decline in the population. Investment is necessary for this, but opinions differ on the extent of bureaucratic leadership required. Inflation is likely to remain somewhat higher due to fiscal policy, so the pattern of compensation via a range of subsidies and tax cuts will likely continue. At this point there is still ample fiscal leeway, but once this is consumed there will be less of a buffer for additional spending in the case of a natural disaster or the like. In any case, the government needs to demonstrate to the market that fiscal policy is not excessive. It is appropriate to reduce the debt/GDP ratio and desirable that the pace of the decline at least be maintained. Because of the recent rates sell-off, the forwards are now approaching the cap levels, which would cause the holders of the floaters to take on unexpected duration and short vega risk. We believe some of these investors have either bought intermediate expiry swaptions to hedge the exposure or sold the floaters outright, in which case the dealers likely would have hedged the short vol exposure. The announcement of an early election and the ensuing policy uncertainty is a net negative for SPGB-Bund spreads. Ordinarily, we think this should be only a mild headwind for spreads as the potential fiscal and political outcomes, according to the polls, are quite narrow, unlike in countries such as France. However, at the moment markets are being driven more by flows and the escalation in the Middle East rather than fundamentals, as we saw with OATs and BTPs last week, with speculative carry trades being stopped out. The price action has even dragged SPGBs wider, including the front-end, which until recently had been trading as a lower beta asset. We reiterate our view that long term, Spain is a fiscal and economic outperformer in the EGB space, something we identified in Eurozone: Political bumps on the road to fiscal convergence, dated 10 September, with low starting debt levels, strong nominal growth and primary balances well in surplus, which are needed to stabilize debt/GDP. Early parliamentary elections in Spain could in theory even be bullish for SPGB spreads in the long run. Naturally, expenditure could well be larger than this. There are many request items for which amounts are not indicated, and given also an increase in defense spending under the government’s three national security documents, subsidies to farmers, and transfers to local governments etc., the amount is likely to increase. Toshiba has also reportedly set a medium-term goal of tripling its overall HDD market share to 30% (from ~11% currently), and aims to achieve mass production of 65 TB drives in 2030. If achieved, at face value that would place Toshiba’s technology roadmap in line with Seagate and Western Digital, which currently hold a multi-generation technology advantage. Context and our view: Based on our recent checks with industry experts, we believe Toshiba does intend to expand its HDD production capacity - and this intention is validated by partner TDK’s stated plans to expand head capacity. However, we would also note that at its 2022 Investor Day, Toshiba previously stated its intention to expand production, reach 25% market share by 2025 (from 17% at the time), and ramp 40TB capacity drives in the same timeframe - none of which came to fruition (vs. Toshiba’s current share of 11%). However, given the HDD industry is both dramatically more profitable and growing faster today, we believe Toshiba is highly motivated to take advantage of these market conditions - and will likely attempt to execute on these plans. records.text: Europe. We consider EU-wide IP data at the granular sub-industry level and identify seven subcategories that are particularly exposed to the AI investment cycle. Production in these areas is clearly outperforming the rest of the manufacturing sector, with growth rates comparable to those observed in areas that are benefitting from increased defence spending (Exhibit 8). Over the last 12 months, activity in AI investment-exposed sectors outperformed the rest of the industrial sector by just over 5pp. Given an approximate share in total manufacturing production of around 6% and scaling for the manufacturing share in total GDP , we estimate an approximate contribution from faster IP growth to EU-wide GDP growth of around 0.05pp (Exhibit 9, left). Given the lack of similarly granular data on construction, we are unable to separately estimate a construction impulse from monthly series and thus assume the same contribution from building activity estimated in our bean counting exercise, for a total effect of slightly less than 0.10pp on region-wide GDP growth this year (Exhibit 9, right). As a consequence, the market would probably start to price the risks of a downgrade into the BBB bucket (well ahead of any potential action from rating agencies). In that scenario, France’s fiscal score could indeed dangerously approach BBB-consistent levels (Figure 2) but would still remain far off from levels consistent with worse credit ratings, where non-linearities can rise a lot more. How much is worth a BBB-rated country? One needs to look through history to understand the cost of this transition as the spline can be more or less convex, with a slope more or less flat, depending on the broader risk backdrop. Up until recently, the spline was actually no longer convex, and even the slope in the linear portion had flattened dramatically, symptomatic of a multi-year risk-on markets where carry has long been a preference. Through the course of September, the slope has started to resteepen, driven by both ends; this is evidence of a market starting to price a pick-up in sovereign risk premia. Using monthly averages since 2015, our credit spline analysis suggest a range of 80-150bp over Germany for a BBB+ rated country. Using dailies, 160-170bp cover most of the highs since 2014. We therefore think that a more realistic outcome may be an exemption with a low cap – perhaps JPY5mn per heir, for example, in line with life insurance benefits. A small incentive may sound like a limit support for JGB the but, we can also argue that JGB market may be better supported by a sustained tax revenues. Sales of retail JGBs have increased fast (Figure 1). For FY2026, the government is likely to sell 70% more than the budgeted amount, at about JPY10trn. However, in an environment of global monetary policy tightening, contributing to an already wide rate differential, SEK appears vulnerable. Every 1% depreciation of the trade-weighted exchange rate index likely adds around 5bp to Sweden inflation, according our estimates, but Riksbank research suggests that the pass-through could be as large as 60bp for every 1% TWI move in times of elevated inflation and geopolitical uncertainty . We therefore doubt that the Riksbank can completely decouple from other central banks. Moreover, the improved growth outlook in Sweden, with the consumption recovery now finally on track, also removes the need for monetary policy accommodation. As a result, adjusted our call and brought the expected tightening forward, with the first 25bp hike now expected for November (instead of December). Afterwards, we think the Riksbank will pause in December but hike a second time to (an unchanged) terminal rate of 2.25% in Q1 2027, bringing policy to a likely neutral stance. records.text: Paul Gabard 7 October 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General The Nordic Gap Starts to Close Norway and Sweden have rarely been this far apart on monetary policy. Norges Bank hiked to 4.50% in September, and the same morning the Riksbank held at 1.75%, the lowest policy rate in the EU. At 275bp, the policy gap is unusually wide, but there are growing signs it could start to narrow. The Riksbank's tone has turned hawkish quickly, Swedish prices are starting to move higher, and the data has swung in Sweden's favour. Norges Bank, meanwhile, looks nearly done. Over the next 6–12 months we expect the Riksbank to do more of the hiking, and the front end of the rates curve looks like the cleanest place to express that. A sudden change of tone in Stockholm . The clearest shift has come in what the Riksbank i s saying. A month ago, our MediaStats hawkish/dovish indicator had it at 0.0 0, 11th in our ranking. It now scores 0.33, third in the G10 behind only the RBNZ and the BOE. Norges Bank hasn't moved from 0.00 (Figure 1). The September hold came with a clear message that a hike this year has become more likely and the Riksbank's own path now points to a policy rate averaging around 1.85% in Q4. We expect the global mine deterioration to accelerate over the balance of 2026, with H2-26 production contacting by roughly 6% y/y. For the full year, we expect global zinc mine supply to contract by 2.3%. Chinese mine production has been an exception this year, growing by about 5% y/y in H1. We forecast full-year 2026 growth of around 3.4%. This mine supply growth has also been keyto enabling China’s strong domestic refineryoutput YTD. Modest mine recovery projected for 2027: We forecast a 2.6% pickup in 2027 mine supply. In Peru, we see a modest uptick, from 1.34 Mt this year, to 1.4 Mt next year, with stabilising production at Antamina a key factor. For China, we expect mine supplyto grow 4.9% in 2027, with notable growth from InnerMongolia. There may be significant impact In short, the government would need to consider carefully how much the tax advantages of JGBs would affect other assets, if at all. Trade-off between tax revenue, lower yields: We try to have a sense of tax impact if JGBs are made exempt from inheritance tax. As an example, we assumed an average rate of 30% and an additional JGB sales of JPY20trn of JGBs. JPY 20trn is about twice the current annual retail JGB sales and is similar to the assessed value for 2025 inheritance tax. The impact is mechanically calculated as JPY 20trn x 30% = JPY 6trn and translates to an about 50bp interest cost on the JPY1,200trn of JGBs outstanding (see Figure 5 for JGB interest rate payment and average percentage). Therefore, unless the MoF thinks a full inheritance-tax exemption would lead to a more than 50bp reduction in interest rates, it would be better off not changing the rules from a pure tax revenue perspective. Such a simplified calculation is not everything, of course, but would still matter. In sum, we would think that the realistic solution may be to allow a capped deductible allowance in line with that seen for life insurance (JPY5mn per heir), which is quite small. The advantage for the ECB of the OMT, is that it would put the onus squarely on Paris – since a credit line needs to be requested – as opposed to the decision sitting in Frankfurt. We would not be surprised if President Lagarde – if asked at the October ECB meeting – emphasises that both tools are available and suggests that the TPI could deal with spillovers while OMT is more suited to countries with unsustainable fiscal policies. records.text: Swatch Group - limited scale could slow margin rebound, initiate at Sell, price target CHF174 We initiate with a Sell rating and a 12-month price target of CHF174, with a DCF-derived value of CHF164 and an M&A value of CHF232, respectively accounting for 85% and 15% of our TP . The group spans all price points in watches, from the Swatch brand itself all the way to Breguet and Blancpain, and is slightly more exposed than peers to China and the Middle East, which have been tough markets. The group’s exposure to the watch category and to wholesale channels (c50% of sales) has made growth particularly volatile, and its commitment to maintaining production capacity despite lower demand has meaningfully impacted inventory levels and margins. While 2026 should see a decent sales rebound, valuation is demanding, in our view, and the company’s relatively smaller scale implies that cost of growth would have an impact on the rebuild of sustainably high margins. records.text: 5 October 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 Circuit breakers To sum up, OATs are now cheap under the same valuation framework that identified them as being very expensive post -GFC. There is also evidence of positioning dynamics that could lead to a self -reinforcing widening of OAT spreads, especially at the front end of the curve. Finally, the RN, which is currently leading in the polls, has shifted towards a more conservative fiscal stance and opened the door to the adoption of the current budget. Taken together, the evidence points towards an overshoot in OAT spreads. What are the possible circuit breakers? The ECB has developed a post -GFC toolbox to enable it to deal with unwarranted tightening of financial conditions. It has demonstrated its flexibility on numerous occasions in engineering credit easing via the TLTROs (which are a way of decentralising liquidity provision) and the PEPP (which allowed bond purchases away from capital keys). It has since enshrined some of these tools in the TPI. Ultimately, any ECB intervention is predicated on its assessment of unwarranted and disorderly market dynamics. The flattening of the spread curve was a key element that triggered Draghi’s “whatever it takes” moment and the OMT. records.text: Corporate considerations - points investors raise when evaluating luxury shares Except for Burberry, which is the only company in our luxury coverage that has 100% free float, all of the luxury companies we cover in this report are partly owned and run by family members. This could be viewed as a key positive by long-term investors as (theoretically) controlling shareholders are well positioned to drive investment decisions that are supportive of brand equity building in the long term. At the same time, a shorter-term investor may have different priorities vs longer-term family considerations. Below, we highlight some of the topics linked to listed companies in the space where there have been frequent questions from investors: Succession planning For those companies with significant family involvement, there is always a theoretical question surrounding leadership continuity following the retirement of the current management teams. For instance, this was a recurring question for Richemont prior to the appointment of a non-family CEO in June 2024, working alongside the chairman and controlling shareholder. It was also the case for Kering prior to the appointment of an external CEO, who joined the group after a long career in the autos industry. The question of succession planning appears to be less prominent at companies such as Hermès, given the current leadership structure, or Moncler, which recently brought in an external CEO. records.text: ot straightforward. The TPI, first and foremost, is a monetary policy tool. Its purpose is to ensure that the ECB’s policy is transmitted evenly across the euro area. It is not intended to underwrite a member state’s fiscal policy choices or ease the burden on governments. This is why its activation requires “unwarranted” and “disorderly” market dynamics that present a “serious” risk to the transmission of monetary policy – a deliberately high bar. Wider spreads alone do not constitute disorderly dynamics, and to the extent that wider OAT–Bund spreads partly reflect a deteriorating fiscal outlook, are not necessarily unwarranted (at least directionally) either. At the time of writing, the likely threshold for intervention has not been reached, in our view. The threshold is inherently impossible to quantitatively pin down, as it does not depend on a level of spreads but on a holistic judgement call. A political problem for an apolitical institution: TPI eligibility (see Figure 1, page 10 for more) requires compliance with the EU fiscal framework, the absence of severe macroeconomic imbalances, a sustainable debt trajectory and “sound and sustainable” macroeconomic policies. However, these are non- binding and ultimately the decision on TPI activation rests with the ECB’s Governing Council. records.text: Smooth management transition For the first time since Remo Ruffini bought the Moncler brand in 2003, the group appointed an outside CEO, with Leo Rangone joining in April 2026. Mr. Rangone has a strong track record in luxury, having served in leadership positions at several of the larger groups, notably Fendi (LVMH) as well as Saint Laurent and Bottega Veneta (Kering). Around the same time, Moncler saw the departure of its longtime chief commercial officer and head of marketing. More recently, the group appointed a new European head, formerly CEO of brands Jil Sander and K-Way. We see the management transition strengthening stability – addressing longer-term succession planning – and focus for the group, for the first time creating a clear separation of operational and creative leadership which enables Mr. Ruffini, in the newly created position of Executive Chairman, to focus on creative direction and strategic vision. The question of cash management Moncler, given its high margins and despite the investment in Stone Island, should end the 2026 year with a net cash position of €1.68bn on our estimates, a sizable 14% of market cap. Given the under-penetrated nature of the US market for the group and the early stages of development of Stone Island (which in our view will likely require a retail ramp-up starting in 2028 following a period of clean up), we see these as the main demands on cash. records.text: ‘Inside the model’: Growth above the average, but below history Sales After delivering 6% organic growth in 1H26, we see Hermès continuing to grow ahead of the sector but no longer at the double-digit pace investors have historically become accustomed to. While Leather Goods remains the key growth engine (we forecast c.10% growth for FY26E and close to 10% thereafter, with an implied low-single-digit price and 6%-7% volume contribution), momentum across the rest of the portfolio looks increasingly mixed. Categories such as Ready-to-Wear & Accessories, Watches and Perfumes have all seen a notable moderation in growth, which we believe reflects weaker demand from more aspirational customers and greater competitive intensity. As a result, we forecast Group organic sales growth of c.7% on average for FY26-28E. While this remains industry-leading on our forecasts, it is a meaningful step down from the growth algorithm investors have historically associated with the brand and, in our view, puts pressure on Hermès’ valuation premium, particularly if competitors close the performance gap following two years of underperformance. Our FY26-28 sales estimates are modestly below Visible Alpha Consensus Data. Operating profit We see some scope for slight gross margin expansion. The 2 October price action emphasised just how much global developments matter, even on a day marked initially by sharp OAT underperformance. A weak US labour print provided a circuit breaker: Global duration rallied and 10y OAT–Bund spreads tightened from 156bp to 141bp intra-day. In light of this, we note that a temporary resolution in the Middle East alongside factors that send yields lower could act as tightening drivers for OATs. Flows versus fundamentals: Price action in the past week in particular has been flow driven, rather than signalling a change in the fundamental picture for France, in our view. Ordinarily, spread widening driven by fiscal concerns has tended to be led by longer maturities such as the 10y point. Last week, 2y and 5y spreads out-widened the 10y point, resulting in a sharp collapse of the 2s10s and 5s10s boxes. A blowout in front-end spreads can sometimes be reminiscent of default risk historically, but this was not the case last week. We think speculative longs in the 1y–5y sector for carry were stopped out or unwound in France and Italy. To add to this, we also observe that for most of September, the sell-off was futures led, likely driven by speculators, by hedging needs related to repacks, and by technical factors such as a CTD switch on the OATZ6 contract which amplified the sell-off on the 10y point.

records.text: From a brand simplification story to a quality luxury asset In recent years, Zegna has gone through a period of a simplification at its Zegna brand and has seen an improvement in the quality of its revenues. Historically, investors struggled with a business that had a higher reliance on wholesale, greater exposure to China, and unclear positioning at its core Zegna brand. Today, the picture is very different. Through a deliberate rationalization of wholesale distribution, the Group has increased the share of its revenues generated through DTC channels from c.73% in FY23 to c.85% in 2Q26, improving its control over distribution, pricing and customer engagement, while supporting a meaningful improvement in its revenue quality and gross margin. At the same time, the company has reduced its exposure to China while growing its presence in the US, making the geographical split more balanced, and improving resilience and visibility through the recent luxury downturn. Relative to peers, we believe Zegna stands out for three reasons: First, Zegna remains the most vertically integrated business in the sector. The Group manufactures >60% of its products in-house, and retains significant control over its manufacturing capabilities and textile expertise, reflecting its roots as a fabric producer. Deflation and disinflation were themes around the world, and monetary policy converged. Central banks put in place low or negative interest rate policies, and QE caused their balance sheets to swell. There was a change in the trend toward compressed risk premia, and inflation driven by the novel coronavirus pandemic caused rate hikes to levels above what had previously been expected. With YCC in place at the time the BoJ’s first move was tardy, but the 10y bond yield has caught up over the past year. Looked at in this context, Japan was simply catching up to other countries until the yield reached 3%, and interest rates were in any case moving in an upward direction with little influence from the external environment. In short-term interest rates as well, the BoJ’s rate hikes were seen as behind the curve, and they did not have the expected effect on the forex market. Short-term interest rates are still low, but this does not apply to long-term rates. The reverse could now be true with movements in the market meaning Japan has an effect on other nations. Risk premia are likely to vary between countries depending upon inflation and fiscal positions. Markets are likely to be impacted most by energy prices in the near term. records.text: in recent years, funding conditions remain benign, and balance sheet constraints have eased, compressing the opportunity set in Treasury RV and basis arbitrage. At the same time, higher rates and volatility have increased uncertainty around CTD outcomes and the embedded option value in Treasury futures. • Trading the basis means trading future CTD outcomes. The basis narrows for bonds moving toward CTD status and widens for those moving away. Basis performance moves with rates. Higher rate vol also increases the value of the option embedded in Treasury futures. • Empirical DV01 already prices CTD extension in WN, US has room to go. In US, the CTD has room to extend further out the curve towards the 2050 sector in a larger sell-off, which would push the empirical DV01 higher. We estimate asset managers' gross rebalancing needs at about $25m DV01 in US and $3mm DV01 in WN. The basis — More than an arbitrage trade The traditional arbitrage relationship between futures and cash basis has compressed this year. Improved liquidity conditions, a benign funding environment, and increased dealer balance sheet capacity following SLR reform have narrowed the relative value opportunity set for basis trades (see here). Pricing along the Treasury curve has become more efficient with fewer dislocations for investors to exploit, especially with the Treasury increasing long-end buybacks. To this end, and as early as November 2021, group Chairman Patrizio Bertelli mentioned that the group could explore a listing in Europe, while making it clear that this was not a priority. That message has been reiterated by CEO Andrea Guerra and CFO Andrea Bonini ever since. The group’s finance team moved to reporting quarterly in May 2023 (for that year’s Q1), possibly to improve investor visibility and better align with practices from luxury sector peers. The group CEO reiterated in May 2024 that a Milan listing was not a priority, and explained that the technicalities of a dual listing were one of the reasons against it. Those technicalities possibly include considerations of Italy’s settlement system, regulatory disclosure, prospectus documentation and more. The topic of the share listing also comes hand in hand with questions of a capital raise, or indeed any other way of increasing the float (limited trading is another reason investors are not looking at Prada’s shares as intently as we believe they should). In January 2026, HKEX’s public-float rules were changed, enabling a listed company in Hong Kong (such as Prada) to use an alternative threshold principle to limit its free float to 10%, instead of the previous 20%. records.text: As we head into 3Q26 earnings, we expect investors to focus on three key themes: 1) the outlook for capital markets after a strong 2Q26, with 3Q26 equities trading expected to normalize QoQ, pockets of weakness in FICC given the move in rates and a much slower investment banking quarter, although still up YoY; 2) the outlook for NII amidst strong loan growth, coupled with fixed rate asset repricing, partially offset by higher deposit costs; 3) the prospects for capital deployment to moderate from here, driven by lower levels of excess capital, the AOCI impact from higher rates, and pressure from three consecutive years of G-SIB buffer increases. Valuation for the group appears fair, after the 5% decrease in share prices in 3Q26, driven by multiple derating. The average FY+2 P/E multiple now stands at the ~50th percentile and the group is trading at 60% of the S&P 500 multiple (1pp below the historical level). We expect that large cap banks will continue to generate attractive ROTCEs in the near term given the strong revenue environment and benign credit outlook, although a multiple re-rating is dependent on greater clarity around the macro and the shape of the rates curve in particular. Scenario 1: a quick resolution In the first scenario, there would be a relatively quick resolution of the conflict, and flows through the Strait of Hormuz would rapidly recover further. This would be a similar outcome to the June MoU, which would further improve market confidence and support a recovery in regional energy exports. While some logistical bottlenecks persist initially, supply chains normalise over the course of 4Q26, and no major oil infrastructure is permanently damaged. Overall demand would rebound relatively quickly as the risk premium recedes and prices move lower. The further return of tanker flows from the Gulf would likely bring prices down rapidly, but keeping them at around $80/bbl in 4Q26, as inventory replenishment provides support to physical demand and limits further downside risk, before falling to $75/bbl in both 2027 and 2028. Scenario 2: Base Case - gradual normalisation Our base case assumes that the conflict in the Gulf does not end immediately, but conditions gradually improve and flows through the Strait of Hormuz progressively return towards normal by the end of 1Q27. The recovery is slower and less orderly than in Scenario 1, with shipping conditions, insurance availability and regional production taking time to normalise

Attacks on ships in the Strait are reported daily, and shipping costs from the Gulf have risen to $20-30+/bbl. Meanwhile, Iranian exports have dropped to zero for several weeks as the US blockade remains very effective. This increases the risk of escalation in the near term, in our view, and we could see renewed targeting of energy infrastructure across the region. Recent attacks on the Saudi East- West pipeline are a reminder of the risks around bypass routes as well. Risk still slightly skewed to the upside in the absence of political resolution Despite the recovery in flows, we still see risks as slightly skewed to the upside for oil prices in the very near term, given the potential for further escalation and a reduced inventory buffer. We provide more detailed scenario analysis within the note. New attacks and disruptions to flows could send prices to $120+/bbl. The main downside risk is a return to the MoU and greater stability around Middle East flows. This could take prices below $80/bbl more quickly than we model. The four questions on which overseas investors in London concentrated were BoJ cadence, the level of the yen, GPIF and the issuance plan. Our visits fell in the week of 21 September, when US and European yields surged while Tokyo was closed for a three-day holiday. The 10y Treasury yield rose above 5.1% to its highest since 2007 and the 10y Bund to its highest since 2009, and JGBs imported the move in a single session on Thursday. In that environment, overseas investors' view on yen rates was neither bullish nor bearish but broadly neutral. When and how far does the BoJ go next? At what yen level do the authorities act? Will GPIF change its Basic Portfolio? And where in the curve will extra issuance land? Every one of them is a question about sequence and landing spot rather than about the level of yields, and there was little disagreement on levels themselves. On the BoJ, most investors expected the next hike in December as long as the yen stays at 157 to 159. records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Visible exchange inventory up 52% YTD: Combined metals exchange (LME + SHFE) inventory currently stands at about 270 Kt, up 52% from the start of 2026. The bulk of the growth, unsurprisingly, has occurred in China, where visible volumes have jumped by 105% over the last nine months and stand at 146 Kt. LME volumes have risen by only 15%, with volumes now at 124 Kt, all of which is in Asia LME warehouses (and almost 50% of Chinese origin). Total visible stocks currently provide for roughly seven days of global demand coverage. Much of China’s August exports appear to have gone into LME warehouses in Asia, we believe, where volumes have risen by c.38Kt since YTD lows of 86.5 Kt on 18 August. With more exports expected in September and October, we anticipate more LME deliveries . Chinese deliveries key to easing LME spread tightness in late September: Chinese deliveries into the LME explain why the LME zinc spread fell from a backwardation of USD230/t to USD50/t between 27 August and 22 September. This sharp fall was partly reversed by the Trafigura announcement to place the Auby zinc smelter in France under review. Whilst we expect more deliveries, the volumes and delivery rates are insufficient to enable a rebalancing between an oversupplied Chinese market and an undersupplied ex-China, in our view. Visible exchange inventory is rising (+49% y/y) on Chinese oversupply beginning to be exported.

records.text: European sovereign risk is back in focus, with French 10-year bond spreads rising n to the highest level since 2012. While sovereign concerns have mainly focused on France, signs of spillovers into other bond markets have emerged, raising questions around the potential implications for ECB policy. First, tighter financial conditions could have implications for the ECB’s hiking n cycle. Our Euro area financial conditions index (FCI) has tightened by nearly 40bp since the start of July, potentially substituting for one 25bp ECB rate hike. We maintain our forecast for a third and last hike in December, but tighter financial conditions reduce the urgency to raise rates beyond this, strengthening our view that the Governing Council is unlikely to step up the pace of hikes or take rates significantly restrictive. Second, the Governing Council could lean against further sovereign stress by n slowing the pace of balance sheet runoff. One option would be a return to partial reinvestments (which could be used flexibly); another would be to introduce new purchases to build the planned structural bond portfolio. While potentially helpful for mitigating fragmentation risk, changes to the balance sheet runoff policy would likely be controversial and require further signs of bond market stress. First, while less prominent than elsewhere, local data centre build out should have a modest positive effect on European growth via increased activity in construction and fitting, even if the computing hardware is largely imported (Exhibit 3, left). Second, Europe should benefit from increased demand for AI-exposed goods, including semiconductor-related capital goods, electronics, and electrical equipment. Indeed, business surveys in these sectors point to export and production expectations at or close to historical highs (Exhibit 3, right). In this Analyst, we thus review the evidence of these two channels and employ three different approaches to estimate the likely contribution of the global AI capex cycle to European GDP growth. Modelling Spillovers with Input-Output Table First, we adopt a model-driven approach that leverages input-output tables to capture direct effects and spillovers from the global AI cycle. To do so, we leverage detailed metrics on the composition of US AI hardware spending compiled by our Global team colleagues by replicating the US national accounts commodity-flow method of estimating investment. Their approach enables us to break down US AI spending by component and to track how much of that is resulting from higher net imports as opposed to increased domestic production. Changes of ECB haircuts for CB - significant impact unlikely As announced last year, the ECB has now updated its valuation haircuts for CB used as repo collateral, effective from 30 Nov onwards (link, link). Within the AAA to A range, there are only small changes of up to 1 percentage point. In the hardly relevant BBB CB segment, the changes are larger but typically lead to lower haircuts (except for maturities of 30y plus). However, the haircuts for own-use CB will change significantly. Instead of adding 8% (AAA-A) or 12% (BBB) to the standard valuation haircut, the ECB introduces a separate haircut schedule for own use CB. While the haircuts for (the hardly relevant) own -use BBB CB segment will decline over all maturity buckets, the haircuts for the AAA-A rated long dated CB will go up markedly. For example, the haircut for 30y plus fixed or floating CB will increase from 18% to 28% and those for 15 -30y fixed or floating CB will increase from 16% to 22%. However, in shorter maturities, for example 1-3y fixed and floating CB, the haircut will increase only from 9.5% to 10%. records.text: How we derive our price targets We use a DCF valuation for all of our coverage For the entirety of our luxury coverage - we initiate on 9 stocks in this report - we value using a DCF. For all companies, regardless of where they are listed, we use the same risk free rate of 3.65%, a reflection of the developed markets in which they are based. We also use the same ERP of 4.85%, which is a combination of Eurozone, US and China rates, equally weighted, given we consider the companies as global in nature. As shown in the exhibit below, the key differences between the stocks in the sector are: - our perception of risk and volatility, expressed by company-specific beta - the balance in terms of debt versus equity, and - the long-term growth rate, which we see mostly as a function of the companies’ underlying businesses. For instance, we believe Richemont, being mainly a jeweler, should grow more in the long term than Swatch, which is essentially exposed to the watch category. We use a sector beta of 1.25, which reflects the risk that investors currently perceive in luxury given volatile growth, a tough macro set-up in China, and the general wait-and-see attitude of many consumer cohorts across the globe, with the possible exception of US and South Korean top-tier consumers. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals5 October 2026 ab 2 Global Oil Fundamentals UBS Research Global Oil Market UBS Scenario We expect Brent to average $100/bbl over the rest of the year. While flows through the Strait of Hormuz and bypass routes have got closer to normal, the recovery remains fragile given ongoing Iranian attack. Normalisation has been delayed and we also believe that the market is likely to factor in a structurally higher risk premium to a certain extent, as tensions are likely to linger. A limited supply response and the need to rebuild inventories should also support prices in 2027. Looking further out, rising efficiency and EVs' increasing impact should see demand growth slow sharply and peak oil reached by 2030, although this is likely to be followed by a long plateau rather than a sharp drop. We expect global spare capacity to decline as non-OPEC supply growth slows down more rapidly than oil demand growth, limiting the negative impact on prices and keeping long-term marginal cost around $75/bbl. The S&P 500 trades just 1% below its record high reached in mid-August but the median S&P 500 stock trades 16% below its respective 52-week high. In contrast, Europe doesn’t have the concentration in a few stocks (Exhibit 5) and breadth has been only a little lower than average (Exhibit 6). Why come to Europe? What we like about the category, however, is that, unlike ready-to-wear or footwear, there is little pressure linked to obsolescence and the need to carry different sizes, which limits the risk of discounting and any reliance on disposition channels, whether in outlets or online, both of which we believe can weigh on brand equity over the short and long term. Also, while price increases have been somewhat more measured in luxury jewelry (even leading to some gross margin disappointment at Richemont), perceived “greedflation” has been a much bigger issue for handbags, which made the post COVID normalisation phase for the segment more challenging. Following a period of changes in designers and CEOs, we have now seen many of the brands rebuild their pricing and product architecture, leading to what we believe should be a convincing pick-up in growth next year. While frequent data is not available for Chanel as it is a privately held company that only reports once a year, the company, despite its large scale, appears to be making a strong comeback in leather and accessories, standing out as somewhat of an exception for now. The 10y OAT -Bund spread briefly touched 150bp on Friday, its highest since 2012 during the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis. The latest leg of the move looks to be less a reflection of fundamentals – which have not suddenly deteriorated even though they remain weak – and more stop-out-driven selling. Our fundamental analysis suggests that 150bp on 10y OAT-Bund spreads would be a level consistent with the market pricing a country going towards BBB+, levels reached briefly on Friday. However, for a sustained rally in OAT spreads where fundamentals start to reassert themselves, we would need: i) positioning to be cleared out, especially front-end longs; ii) the budget in France to pass this year, with the social security vote in November an important test; iii) strong OAT auctions as an important source of price discovery and demand ; iv) greater details on the RN’s fiscal consolidation plan, expected in the coming week; v) a shift in the French opinion polls. Meanwhile, we think that there is a high bar for the ECB to step in and use its ‘Transmission Protection Instrument’, which was unveiled in 2022 but remains untested. The tool is designed to counter both “unwarranted” and “disorderly” market moves that “seriously” impair the transmission mechanism of monetary policy. records.text: Margins: LVMH again displayed tight cost discipline; H1 EBIT margin came out nicely ahead (70bps) of expectations At a time of lackluster sales growth, the group managed to beat margin expectations in all five divisions with very strong - though in our view likely unsustainable - performance in Wines & Spirits and, importantly, very good resilience in the key Fashion & Leather division (which accounted for 71% of group EBIT in the half). This is a manifestation of, in our view, a changed culture within the group, as well as an important step in putting an end to downward revisions to consensus earnings estimates. What to expect from the Q3 2026 trading statement For the Q3 trading statement (likely published the week of October 12, 2026), we project modest 1% organic sales growth at the group level (vs. 3% in Q2), partly as the basis of comparison is a little tougher and partly on account of unfavourable macro data in China. We see the key profit driver, the Fashion & Leather division, being down 2.5%. This, in itself, is unlikely to be very inspiring, though we project a better Q4 (flat), and importantly, an acceleration in 2027 (+4%) as product portfolio renewals compensate more pedestrian growth at LV (c+2%). In Q3, we also factor in a sequential slowdown, relative to Q2, for Wines & Spirits, as well as Watches & Jewellery, but see Selective Retail going strong at +5.5%. Reading that as "the belly is rich" ignores the asymmetric spacing of the wings: the midpoints of the three forwards are 1.5, 3.5 and 7.5 years, so the belly is two years from the front wing and four years from the back wing. On a straightforward curve the fly equals minus two times the slope per year. With the slope at 22bp per year (129bp from 1y1y to 5y5y over six years) the straight-line value is -43bp, and the +6bp difference from the actual -37bp is the curvature: the belly sits 3bp above the chord joining the wing midpoints (2.70% at 3.5 years), or 6bp cheap in fly terms (Figure 60). There is no valley, only slope. records.text: rtier started in 1969 with a bracelet before the brand added rings, pendants, earrings, a smaller version (Mini Love in 2016) and a flexible version (the successful Love Unlimited product, introduced in late 2025). In other words, icons start as a recognisable design and, if managed appropriately, become fully fledged families of products that customers can relate to. The only distinction we would make between an icon (product design) and a code is that the latter can relate to a colour (e.g. black and white, as well as beige, at Chanel, red at Cartier, Valentino or Louboutin, robin’s-egg blue at Tiffany, Black at Saint Laurent, Grey at Dior etc.), a pattern (e.g. the monogram at LV, GG canvas at Gucci, Burberry checks, Dior Oblique), a production technique (e.g. embroidery at Gucci, epi leather at Louis Vuitton, re-nylon or Saffiano leather at Prada) or any other recurring pattern that consumers typically associate directly with a given brand. Within the bigger brands, we have seen Tiffany shift rapidly towards re-calibrating its offering around icons (with success), while Burberry recently refocused on existing icons that had possibly not benefited previously from greater attention. Dior stands out, in our view, as having the greatest potential in building further its franchise by establishing additional icons alongside its main, historical Lady Dior range. What to watch? We outlined a roadmap to SNB hikes in our latest Switzerland quarterly. Drawing on past hiking cycles, we think the sequencing includes somewhat higher spot inflation (around 1%), a notably higher end-point of the SNB’s inflation forecast (around 1.75%) and further CHF weakness (possibly as weak as 2023 levels if domestic price pressures remain absent). What to watch: ECB meeting (29 October), SNB Watchers Conference (5 November). Strategy implication FX strategy: The OAT-Bund spread widening of last week has triggered a sharp squeeze in CHF shorts, and driven EURCHF back into the recent range. Last week we shifted from bullish CHF to modestly bearish, largely due to the more dovish than anticipated SNB Sep meeting outcome reinforcing the already compelling case for using CHF as a funding currency for long carry positions. But we did not recommend going short CHF due to positioning being very one sided. With the build-up in short franc positions now likely greatly reduced, the risk reward to being long EURCHF is improving; but for the trade to be attractive, ECB tightening expectations need to be resilient and vol conditions benign. In the meantime, we continue to see USDCHF upside as supported by the US rate profile and energy prices and target 0.85 by year-end. Rates strategy: We close

As widely expected, the Riksbank kept the policy rate unchanged at 1.75% in September, but is now guiding for lift-off in Q4. The statement noted that "the combination of stronger economic activity and continued supply shocks means that the policy rate should be raised more than projected in the June forecast" and that "it is expected that the increases to the policy rate will begin this year." The revised policy rate path now indicates a high probability of a hike in November, and the statement notes that the Riksbank also stands ready to "raise the policy rate at a faster pace than in the current forecast" if "there were to be signs of a larger and more persistent upturn in inflation". In recent weeks, ongoing Middle East tensions, a Fed hike and further expected ECB tightening have strengthened the case for Riksbank rate hikes. The economic fundamentals in Sweden are different from the Eurozone and the US, notably more labour market slack and a still negative output gap in Sweden, implying that the Riksbank may not mechanically follow other central banks. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals5 October 2026 ab 9 What is the outlook for Middle East flows? Flows through Hormuz remain highly sensitive to geopolitical developments between the US and Iran. Iran keeps asserting its control through the waterway, but its effective leverage over regional crude exports has diminished as overall flows out of Gulf have progressively recovered. This resilience has been supported by greater utilisation of bypass routes in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Iraq, an increase in dark transit activity and rising ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Meanwhile, the US maintains significant pressure on Iranian exports through its naval blockade, effectively reducing Iranian loadings to zero in September. records.text: European Economics 05 October 2026 Citi Research 2 Italy: Fiscal Obedience Italy presented its updated multi-year fiscal projections (Documento Programmatico di Finanza Pubblica, DPFP) on Friday. Our main takeaways are the following: 1.2026 fiscal deficit still on track for sub-3% - The 2026 budget deficit target was confirmed at 2.9% of GDP (first sub-3% print since 2019), down from 3.1% in 2025. This was by no means certain, considering higher yields (and higher inflation-linked bonds’ servicing costs this year). Confirmation in March 2027 of a sub-3% budget deficit for 2026 would allow Italy to exit the Excessive Deficit Procedure EDP on schedule. We still see some downside risks here (i.e. larger than expected 2026 deficit), given the latest rise in yields and inflation. But overall, the improvement in the primary balance should be confirmed (as it appeared in this morning’s quarterly data up in 2Q26, see Fig 1). Relative to France, the fact that Italy was able to keep its 2026 deficit target (below 3% vs 5.4% in France) and to revise upward its GDP growth forecast (to 1%, vs France’s downward-revised growth to 0.5%) speaks in favour of Italy’s better fiscal dynamics. Italy’s fiscal stance at the moment is supportive of growth through the EU-financed Recovery and Resilience Fund’s spending, in sharp contrast to the French restrictive fiscal stance. Figure 1. records.text: Diminishing returns from a successful repositioning Fewer low-hanging fruits At the time of the arrival of the new CEO at Burberry two years ago, we believe the brand was suffering from overpriced items and unsuccessful collections. At the same time, its core appeal in outerwear had been lost, while the unique Britishness of the brand had been muted among a sea of French and Italian competitors. We see what happened next less as revolutionary, and more as a straightforward return to basics. With new product introductions, a revamped marketing strategy, and more palatable price points, we see the brand as firmly back where it is expected to be, having drawn in many new consumers. Relative to the rest of our coverage, Burberry stands out for three things: First, it is undeniably, once more and first and foremost, an outerwear brand, with trench coats and scarves at its core, rather than a generalist. In that regard, only Moncler might be comparable. The hero is once again the trench, not a handbag. Second, it is a democratic brand with a good / better / best pricing approach, which some might consider more reminiscent of a fast-moving consumer goods company than the higher-end European brands. We see this approach simply as pragmatic and embedded in the brand’s history, where accessibility and well-priced ‘giftables’ have been key drivers. Source: J.P. Morgan, Bloomberg Finance L.P. Market tops are frequently preceded by narrowing participation: the index pushes to new highs while fewer and fewer stocks come along for the ride. We measure this with market breadth, the percentage of S&P 500 members trading above their own 100-day moving average, and watch for it to diverge from price. The signal flags when the index is making a fresh three-month high while breadth sits more than 10% below its own three-month high. In other words, the headline is still climbing, but it is being carried by a shrinking group of leaders while the average stock has already begun to roll over. The red zones below mark where breadth was lagging a new high in price and the S&P 500's trend had already broken. When the index's strength is this hollow and momentum turns with it, the divergence becomes an actionable cue. The first market response would likely be a front -end rally as the market prices a lower expected path for Fed policy. An unwind of the investment boom’s effects, including weaker aggregate demand, easing inflation pressures, and tighter financial conditions, would push both real yields and breakevens lower. Long-end Treasuries would also benefit from weaker growth and safe -haven demand, though, in an orderly slowdown, probably less than the front end. While long-end real rates should decline as growth expectations and estimates of r* fall, term premia could remain high if corporates are expected to continue borrowing heavily to f und the remainder of their long -term commitments, or if fiscal concerns remain elevated. In a disorderly slowdown, markets might also anticipate policy support and public spending to cushion the adjustment, further limiting the long-end rally. The result would likely be a bull steepener, as lower r* and flight -to-quality demand pull long-end yields lower, but elevated term premia limit the extent of the rally. But such preferential treatment is not limited to the primary residence, and property investment has therefore been a popular route to reduce inheritance tax. records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Chinese refined output, strong growth finally prompting strong exports : Chinese zinc smelters have to an extent acted as a cushion against negative spot treatment charges in the form of sizeable, domestic vertically integrated mine supply. China accounts for roughly one-third of global zinc mine supply and meets around two-thirds of China’s smelter zinc concentrate requirements annually, enabling H1-26 Chinese refined production to grow at about 5% y/y. Strong production growth has pushed the domestic Chinese zinc market into a sizeable surplus over 2026, and it was only a matter of time before that sparked an export surge. This duly arrived in August, when 40,668t of refined zinc was shipped, the second highest monthly export volume ever. The export arb window, allowing for physical premia and including VAT etc., opened at start of July. Allowing for handling and freight costs, exporting has been profitable since early August. Despite the export arb window closing towards the end of September, we still expect high export volumes for September and October – but expect a drop in November –December as Chinese smelters cut production rates. More refined output growth in 2027: Over the last 21 months, Chinese smelting capacity has jumped by c.950 kt, to 9.5 Mt. The brand’s heritage in cashmere, with knitwear typically priced at €2,000-4,000, and its focus on craftsmanship, quality and timeless design give it access to a particularly affluent customer cohort that we believe is less sensitive to macro-economic volatility and price increases. records.text: Sluggish demand globally but some regional bright spots and a buoyant American cluster US: An emerging market for luxury... finally For a long time, we have thought that there was a surprising disconnect between wealth in the US (high) and luxury demand among American consumers (low). This was likely a function of limited awareness, cultural barriers (“guilt factor”, outlet culture) and a prolonged focus of brands on Asia resulting in a chronic under-investment in the Americas. Post COVID, there is clear evidence that the appetite of American consumers for luxury products has picked up strongly, with brands leaning in, store openings multiplying, and much greater attention directed towards the market, notably as Europe, China and more recently the Middle East have come under pressure in terms of luxury demand. Of course, broad-based wealth creation, notably driven by equity markets has also helped fuel growth. We do not take a view on US equity markets, but we believe that, unless there is a steep correction, the all-important holiday season in the US should remain supportive of sector sales this year. In an industry where growth is largely driven by the capacity brands have to recruit customers, not necessarily to retain them, while it may sound counterintuitive, we still think the US is an emerging market for luxury goods. Across a variety of scenarios (Figure 1), and including current betting odds, the 10y OAT–Bund spread should trade between 100–150bp, with betting odds closer to 100-130bp (ignoring flows and global factors). In an extreme scenario with Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon priced at 50% each to take the presidency, and with the probability of them gaining a parliamentary majority skewed towards 70%, the 10y OAT– Bund spread would be 197bp. Looking at price action from last week, we think global factors and flows could drive a further 15– 20bp move in either direction. Global factors matter: Since the start of July, the 10y OAT– Bund spread has widened by a significant 61bp. The widening appears to have had two phases. First, a global spread widening, exacerbated by the risk-off from the Middle East and higher yields, in which the 10y OAT–Bund widened around 31bp but Belgian and Italian spreads to Germany were also wider by around 13bp. Second, the emergence of French idiosyncratic risk triggering a contagion to other EMU spreads and a flight to quality on the Bund ASW (Figure 2). Until the first phase, 10y BTP–Bund and OLO–Bund spreads were around 15bp wider from end July to 23 September. And until the second phase kicked in, 10y SPGB–Bund spreads were around 18bp wider. records.text: 95 The excessive German stimulus optimism from Q1 ‘25 has faded, just at the time when spending could show an uplift ◼ Germany (and much of Europe) spent decades under-investing in physical infrastructure: public capex lagged the euro-area average and replacement needs, leaving net public capital broadly flat/declining through the 2010s and creating a backlog across transport, schools, plus weaker digital and grid capacity. This is a multi-year catch-up, not a cyclical top-up. ◼ Fiscal policy is now turning. The structural primary deficit is set to widen from -0.7% of GDP (2025) to -1.8% (2026) and -2.3% (2027) i.e. ~2% of GDP easing over two years. The total federal deficit (incl. Special Funds) stays near ~4% of GDP through 2030. Markets have faded the stimulus trade since Q1, but the €500bn infrastructure fund is real; the issue has been timing/planning. By August 2026, the cumulative federal deficit was already €22bn wider y/y, about half the full-year widening implied by the 2026 budget. As for WN, the CTD sector is in the shortest maturities in the basket. records.text: gement’s approach to staff costs and inventories The Swatch Group prides itself on being a substantial employer in Switzerland (close to 32k employees in 2025) and on retaining staff in tough times in order to be ready when demand rebounds. Preserving Swiss manufacturing capability and skilled labour while accepting lower short-term profitability is, in our view, a deliberate management choice rather than an oversight. The group argues that its financial condition is strong enough to absorb these costs and that it can rapidly increase production when demand recovers. As a comparison, Swatch Group generated close to CHF200k per employee in 2025, while Richemont’s figure was about 2.5x higher. While the staff approach has yielded benefits across several areas, it also has consequences for inventory levels, as shown in the exhibit above, with inventory value in 2025 surpassing sales, as was the case in 2020, an exceptional COVID-affected year. records.text: Louis Vuitton (LV) accounts for 25% of sales and 53% of 2026E EBIT at the group level, in our forecasts. The brand has been through a soft patch over the past two years, with an approach split between one favouring diversification and noise (beauty launch, Murakami collaboration) and one with a more institutional message, centered on the brand’s lifelong connection with ‘the art of travel’. With the nomination of Damien Bertrand as deputy CEO, an uncommon role among LVMH brands, possibly signaling succession planning at LV, we believe there are signs of greater brand coherence. We expect LV’s OSG to decline 1% in 2026, and to grow 2% in 2027. While this is lower than the divisional average we forecast, we see it as a logical outcome from a trade-off between short-term commerciality and long-term brand building and equity enhancement. In other words, while the brand should remain the group’s cash cow, we would expect the controlling shareholders to resist over-exploiting it, doing what’s right for the long term. Very short term (for Q3 2026), we expect the brand to have been under pressure, specifically in China as: (1) it was lapping the opening of ‘The Louis’ (a flagship retail space in Shanghai) a year prior, which had a very positive halo effect on sales in the country; and (2) the Molly Tea backlash (in early July, the bubble tea firm was ordered to pay LV damages following a logo infringement case, putting LV in the news for negative reasons).
